At a nearby grocery store run by Paschur Castelly, who left Haiti 20 years ago, most of the shelves are empty, except for those stocking religious candles and framed pictures of Catholic saints popular with this devout community.
"I can't purchase new merchandise because I don't have people coming in," he said.
"So, our communities, we have doctors, we have engineersâ¦ we came here to get a better life, to help our family in Haiti, you know? Our country doesn't offer us security."
After 20 minutes in the store, the first customer arrived. The man, who asked to remain anonymous, said he had been a warehouse worker for three years.
But like others who have lost TPS, it is likely to mean he has also lost the right to work.
As he chatted with Castelly, he pulled up his right trouser leg and revealed a large ankle monitor.
ICE has said these are part of its Alternatives to Detention programme. "I was given a choice, wear the ankle monitor and report in every two weeks, or sign my deportation order," he said.
As we left the store, Castelly closed the door which he now keeps locked. When a neighbour spotted us and feared an ICE raid, she shouted over to ask if Castelly was okay.

It was a sign of just how much this town remains a symbol - of two versions of America - years after Trump thrust it into the national spotlight, and weeks before voters head to the polls to shape the remainder of his presidency.

"This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"

Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October.
I'd stopped Elisabeth and her friend to ask their thoughts on what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears.
"My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."

But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.
Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.
The president of the National Assembly, YaÃ«l Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.

French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend.

French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.

A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left. It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections.

The mass looting of what's said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?

Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. President Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.

Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts has lead former French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence.

Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's Interior minister Bernard Quintin, warned of the 'TikTokisation' of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liege on "known far left groups".

In France, Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu and his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire," said Nunez. On Tuesday Mr Lecornu spoke of "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups".
Previously he'd accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos.
It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader, Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.

MÃ©lonchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all.

In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians.
"Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa.

But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned."
France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday.
The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics.

MÃ©lenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist Prime Minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy."

MÃ©lonchon went on to apparently imply Mr Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure in public finances."
France is struggling with spiralling public debt and government borrowing costs.

As for intelligence failures on Saturday, President Macron has demanded explanations and a new policing strategy. France's Interior Minister admitted there weren't enough officers on the streets, despite the nationwide protests being publicised well in advance. Following accusations of heavy-handedness at earlier demos, the police seemed very much out of their depth this weekend.
Of all the presidential hopefuls, it would seem Marine Le Pen of the anti-immigration, National Rally Party gains most politically from Saturday's shocking scenes.

She is already way ahead in opinion polls. Le Pen chose to launch a presidential-looking video address to the nation via social media on Sunday. Dressed formally, behind a large desk and in front of a French flag, she blamed Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon by name for his associates who "look to throw the country into chaos," she said.
She also accused the Macron government of "running out of steam", meaning that France was "taken hostage between violence and powerlessness".
She ended her video by reminding French voters they'd have the opportunity to "choose a different path" in 6 months time.
Le Pen's party promotes a law and order, closed border message and, like US President Trump and Vice US President JD Vance, has blamed migrants, amongst others, for the chaos in France on Saturday.
Teacher, Mar, complained that Saturday's violence "suits politicians' purpose. It distracts from weeks of legitimate protests for better public services," she said.

"Politicians aren't listening to what the students need, or what teachers need or what the French people want. They're using the violence to election-campaign to become president and to try to make their opponents look bad."
But increasing numbers in France, many amongst the young Gen Z generation, say they have dwindling faith in "the system".
That's something we see echoed in other European countries where mainly youth-led protests erupted - some violently - this weekend in Italy, Portugal and Albania as well as France and Belgium.
These demonstrations are often triggered by spiralling living costs, deteriorating public services and a sense of powerlessness people feel over their own lives.
What can we do as individuals about our rising energy costs caused by wars far away in the Middle East or in Ukraine, many ask?

Voters increasingly say they are losing faith in traditional or governing political parties to listen to concerns and address them. The young look at climate change, social inequality, impossible housing prices and AI potentially threatening their place in the job market.

According to opinion polls conducted by this year by Pew, 69% of people in France are dissatisfied with democracy. In Spain, it's 68% and in Italy, 62%. (The US is experiencing similar disillusionment with 69% saying they are dissatisfied with how democracy is working.)

So many people I've spoken to in France since Saturday's riots emphasise the importance in making a clear distinction between angry but peaceful protestors, and those intent on wreaking violent havoc.

Politics aside, is what we're now seeing in Europe's protest wave perhaps a powerful cocktail of a bubbling over of frustration, cries for help for the authorities to listen but also, for some, a dark sense there's little left to lose?
Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.

In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.

Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.

Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.

Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.
Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.

According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.

Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel.
With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.
But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.

Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.
Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.
“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.

“This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.

Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.

Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.

Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.

The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.

“The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.

From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.

Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.
Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.
“Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”

Australia’s largest datacentre operator has been forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in Melbourne’s west amid a pause in construction of new 22m power poles following community protest.

On Wednesday, NextDC told the Australian Stock Exchange that delays to electricity provider Jemena’s upgrade of the power poles – essential to delivering the increased electricity required by the expanded West Footscray site – would mean the expansion would be pushed back to the 2027/2028 financial year.

The company’s share price dropped from over $9 per share down to $5.69 per share after exiting the trading halt on Wednesday. Due to the deferred billing and delivery of contracted capacity in M3, the company had reduced its net revenue guidance to between $475m and $500m from between $615m and $640m.

NextDC told the market Jemena had suspended the works due to safety concerns, lack of access to sites arising from community and stakeholder opposition, and due to the local council not approving the building of the 22m power poles – up from 11m today, according to Jemena - while further community consultations take place.

NextDC and Jemena are looking at other options for supplying the increased electricity needs, including alternate locations for poles through industrial zones or connecting via underground power connections.
The expansion of the NextDC site is intended to take it from offering capacity of 60 megawatts today to 225MW, processing power which NextDC has already sold to customers.

The site has faced strong opposition from locals in West Footscray. Guardian Australia reported in May that residents were concerned about the scale of the expansion, the construction noise, and the potential for diesel generators being used in the event of power outages.

The total planned expansion is expected to double the size of the M3 site to 10 hectares when complete. NextDC said construction of the new data halls would continue despite the delay in grid supply from Jemena, but said the Victorian government’s planning decision on a permit for stages six and seven of the construction were taking longer than expected.

NextDC chief executive, Craig Scroggie, told investors in a call on Wednesday that he expects the earliest approval for the expansion would be February 2027, as the Victorian government is about to enter caretaker mode for the 28 November state election.

The application has been with the state government since February 2026, and Scroggie blamed the change of premier from Jacinta Allen to Ben Carroll and the associated cabinet reshuffle for delaying approvals.
Scroggie said it was “disappointing to be facing this particular technical challenge” for M3, but he was confident it could be approved.

“We comply with all of the development requirements under the planning rules. And obviously acknowledging the community concerns more recently, on datacentres, generally, more community consultation is required about… the ongoing operation, development and construction issues on the site.”
West Footscray resident and Citizens of Tottenham member Sean Brown said the community had not set out to reduce shareholder value in raising concerns about the project.
“Our goal was to get a fair outcome for our community and to make sure that proper safety framework is in place – and we still haven’t got those,” he said.
“We’re not stopping. This is continuing until we get a fair outcome for the residents.”
Brown said “whoever forms government” and becomes planning minister after the state election “will be definitely hearing from us”.
“It will be a pretty toxic thing to sign off on.”
Beau Lamarre-Condon played Taylor Swift’s song No Body, No Crime while attempting to dispose of two corpses, a court has heard.
The NSW supreme court has been told he was driving to Bungonia with a friend when the song was played in the van.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

A friend of Lamarre-Condon, known to the court under the pseudonym Elizabeth Kennedy, said she thought she and the officer were going out for lunch when he picked her up on 21 February 2024 – two days after the alleged murders.
He arrived at Kennedy’s home in a white van about 3pm that day, she told the court.
Defence lawyer John Stratton SC on Wednesday suggested Lamarre-Condon told her: “I’m not joking, if you don’t want to help me I completely understand and I won’t be mad”.
He claimed Lamarre-Condon lifted a tarpaulin, which had been stored in the back of the van, and showed Baird’s deceased head.
Stratton said the officer had told her Baird was dead and suggested Kennedy said: “this is like a Taylor Swift song, No Body, No Crime” before playing the song in the car.
She denied Stratton’s suggestions and said he didn’t show her Baird’s body, nor did she choose the song.
“He was the one that put that song on in the car … it’s a very niche song,” she told the court.
“I asked him how he knew it and he said it was from the album, evermore.
“I tried to play a few more songs from the album, evermore, and he didn’t know any of them so it was very weird to me he knew that song.”
Kennedy on Wednesday morning offered her own account of events to the court.
She said she noticed a blue tarp in the back of the van and a lemony smell, like it had just been cleaned.
As Lamarre-Condon took the wheel, the drive got longer and longer, she said.
Every time she asked how much further, he would respond, “just 50 more minutes”. It ended up being a two-hour drive to Goulburn and Bungonia, about 150km away, the court heard.
The van’s windows were open the entire trip and the air-conditioning was on full blast and freezing, Kennedy told the jury.
She said that during the drive he seemed “bubbly” and talked about Swift, who was touring Australia at that time, as well as a Europe trip they were planning together.
They eventually stopped at Bunnings Goulburn, the court heard.

In a statement read to the court on Wednesday morning, a Bunnings sales assistant said he had been approached by two customers that day who claimed they were staying at a friend’s farm in nearby Bungonia and had locked themselves out.
The worker suggested they use an angle grinder.
As Lamarre-Condon and Kennedy went to the Bunnings checkout, the officer asked her to pay for an angle grinder and padlock because he did not have cash with him, she said.
The two then drove to Cella Farm in Bungonia and Lamarre-Condon explained he knew the people who owned the property.
When they arrived, he asked her to put garbage bags over the van’s number plates, but she refused, so he did it himself, Kennedy said.
He then cut the padlock off the gate, cutting himself in the process and asked Kennedy to wait there and not turn on her phone.
“He left me there and drove out of sight behind the house where the bigger dam was,” she told the court.
Kennedy began having a panic attack and, when Lamarre-Condon returned 30 or 40 minutes later, he told her to shush and asked if she had called anyone or turned on her phone.
As they began the return journey to Sydney, he asked if they could go back to Bungonia but she said she needed to be home.
Lamarre-Condon was “weird and cryptic” on the trip back, the court heard.
“It seemed like something went wrong and he wouldn’t tell me about it,” Kennedy told the court.
At one point he almost ran over a bird and said, ‘you know I’d never hurt an animal, right?’, Kennedy said.
Lamarre-Condon attempted to call another police officer friend during the drive.
When the friend didn’t pick up, he said: “‘fuck fuck fuck’ and then he sort of panicked and that’s when he started saying, ‘if I’m quiet, I’m not angry, I’m just thinking’”, the court heard.
He told Kennedy he would have to return to Bungonia and that he would be up all night.
She asked why and he said he could not tell her because he did not want to involve her, the court heard.
He then asked if she could buy him a peach Lipton ice tea as he needed caffeine but didn’t drink coffee.
As she entered the service station to purchase the beverage, he also asked her to fuel up the van, but she couldn’t do it because she didn’t know how to drive or fill up a vehicle.
He was “visibly annoyed” before he swore and jumped out of the car. When asked why he did not want to do it, Kennedy told the court he said he did not want to be on camera.
As they left, she noticed the blue tarp was no longer in the back of the van.
The bodies of Baird and Davies were later found in Bungonia.
The defence team claims Baird and Davies were accidentally shot as the accused acted in “self-defence”.
Lamarre-Condon cleaned up the scene and disposed of the bodies afterwards because he “panicked considerably”, Stratton SC has said.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

A new survey found that close to half of undergraduate students surveyed believe physical violence can be justified to stop "hate speech," as one university president warns that higher education has "lost its way."

In the Buckley Institute's 2026 National Undergraduate Student Survey, 45% of students said violence can be justified to stop what they deem to be hate speech. This includes 54% of liberals, 36% of moderates and 30% of conservatives.

The study also found that 46% of students support shout downs and 40% believe that offensive speech should be subject to criminal prosecution. Additionally, 42% said they would rather live under a socialist system, compared with 28% who chose a capitalist system, and 22% said the U.S. deserved the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Cornerstone University President Dr. Gerson Moreno-Riaño characterized the findings as more of a "moral formation issue" than a matter of free speech, warning that students have developed a "violent entitlement."

"American colleges and universities for a long time now have really ceased to form students morally and are teaching resentment, teaching grievance politics, teaching violent entitlement," he told FOX News Digital. "So when graduates leave these universities, they leave with that. They're not leaving with a moral formation of their hearts, their minds, their lives. They're leaving with resentment."
Moreno-Riaño said that entitlement and resentment are among the reasons why many employers are concerned about the value of a degree.

"It's not just what some will say are worthless degrees. It's also what's behind the degree. Individuals who have been taught to resent, not to reason, not to deliberate, not to have deep conversations with those with whom they disagree," he said.

"Rather, it's grievance, anger, violence, entitlement, and then violent action against it. And that to me is a significant problem. Again, not a free speech issue. It's really about how moral education in higher ed has lost its way. We're training people to be grieved, angry, entitled, violent. And that does not bode well for our democracy and our republic," he continued.
Moreno-Riaño, who has led the private Christian university in Grand Rapids, Michigan, since 2021, emphasized that higher ed has "lost its way" in the U.S. for decades and has become "godless."

"When there is no moral compass in higher ed, there's a vacuum, and what fills it? Ideologies, communism, socialism, grievance, culture. That's what's happened, and it's been happening for years," he said. "Not only that, there's an anti-history bent in higher ed. When you think about today's young students not really knowing the evils of communism, the evils of socialism, and believing it's inspirational, that demonstrates just the moral bankruptcy, but also the academic bankruptcy of these institutions."
Moreno-Riaño argued that some employers may increasingly question the value of hiring college graduates and instead consider training workers directly out of high school.

Moreno-Riaño argued that employers are increasingly concerned about "worthless degrees" that do not prepare the workforce to tackle complicated problems, as well as the ideological bent of many recent college graduates. He warned that many colleges and universities are preparing "socialists and Marxists" who want entitlement and to "destroy the system" rather than "build it, make it, refine it and improve it."

"I think what's happening is that employers are seeing this and many employers are saying, maybe we should train our own people or maybe we should go into the high schools directly and educate the future at the high school level and forget colleges altogether, because colleges are morally bankrupting our future," Moreno-Riaño said.

"I think that's what's happening. And if you combine that with artificial intelligence, you have sharp minds without a moral compass. That's a very dangerous thing because a sharp mind without a moral compass is a weapon looking for a target," he continued.

"For a democracy, we need individuals who can reason, who can deliberate, who can speak with those with whom they disagree and not seek violent action against them, but think deeply about what they're saying, reconsider positions, pursue what is good and with courage. If we don't do that, then we're in trouble. And I think the workplace and employers are seeing that and want to shift that in a different direction," he added.
Moreno-Riaño stressed that American higher education "has to shift," saying it needs to "take moral formation seriously and not be grounded in entitlement and grievance culture."

The Buckley Institute survey, conducted by Inquire LLC, included 803 full-time undergraduate students under age 25 attending four-year public or private colleges and universities. Respondents completed the online survey between Sept. 5 and Sept. 14.

EXCLUSIVE: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has launched a nationwide operation targeting illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently obtaining benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), resulting in multiple arrests, Fox News has learned.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) confirmed the operation to Fox News, announcing several arrests of illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently receiving SNAP benefits.

"Illegal aliens who have no right to be here in the first place are the last people who should be using SNAP benefits and other forms of welfare," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.
"These programs are for Americans only," he continued. "Even non-violent illegal alien crime can still have devastating consequences when they’re defrauding the American taxpayer."

Mullin said those already apprehended and deported by federal authorities represented "just a drop in the bucket," adding that the Trump administration would continue pursuing individuals accused of fraud.
DHS identified several illegal immigrants accused of SNAP fraud, including multiple Haitian nationals.

According to federal officials, Rubstony Junior Theodore, a Haitian national living illegally in the United States, was arrested by ICE as part of the operation. Theodore's criminal history includes arrests for larceny, obstruction of officers and trespassing, DHS said.
Three other Haitian nationals living illegally in the United States — Wilbert Jean Baptiste, Louis Jean and Jhensly Charles — were also arrested, according to DHS.

Elizabeth Povea Rodriguez, a Cuban national living illegally in the United States who was previously convicted of disorderly conduct and arrested on battery and domestic violence allegations, was also arrested, according to DHS.

"These arrests mark the opening salvo in a sustained, large-scale ICE operation specifically targeting illegal aliens who have fraudulently accessed SNAP benefits that American taxpayers fund exclusively for U.S. citizens in need," DHS said.

"Every one of these individuals entered the country unlawfully, then proceeded to draw from a program designed to feed struggling American families, in some cases while carrying criminal records," the agency continued.
Federal law generally bars immigrants living in the country illegally from receiving SNAP benefits, although certain categories of lawfully present noncitizens may qualify for the program.
DHS said the Trump administration would continue targeting alleged SNAP fraud as part of a broader crackdown on misuse of federal benefits.

Dan Lanning said he was still gathering information about Oregon wide receiver Evan Stewart’s arrest but the fifth-year Ducks' head coach vowed to take what he described as "appropriate action" once he had all the necessary details.
"There will be an appropriate action taken. Still gathering some details with what that situation looks like," Lanning said.
He added that the situation would be dealt with internally. "But that would be handled internally. I’m not gonna respond to any other questions about that. We’re gonna handle that with our guys."

Stewart was taken into custody early Sunday on charges of driving under the influence, hours after the Ducks rallied to defeat Nebraska on Saturday night. He was booked into the Springfield Municipal Jail, according to police records.
Lanning said the incident was unfortunate because it cast a shadow on the Ducks’ win.

Stewart did not play in the game against the Cornhuskers because of an undisclosed injury. He has 27 catches for 352 yards and four touchdowns this season after missing all of last season because of a right patellar tendon tear.
"There was an incident this weekend that didn’t match our standard here in our program," Lanning said.
Oregon visits Illinois for a Big Ten matchup with star quarterback Dante Moore’s status still unclear.
Moore has missed the Ducks’ past two games while recovering from a concussion.

Lanning said Moore participated in practice leading up to Oregon’s Week 6 matchup with UCLA, but Brock Thoman and Dylan Raiola ultimately saw action in the Ducks’ 17-15 loss to the Bruins. Both quarterbacks also played against Nebraska.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Current U.S. support for Ukraine looks very different than it did
NPR's Scott Detrow talks with William Taylor, former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine, about President Trump's recent moves to support Russia and how that compares to past administrations.
When Russia first attacked Ukraine nearly five years ago, Joe Biden was president, and the official U.S. response sounded like this.
JOE BIDEN: Putin's aggression against Ukraine will end up costing Russia dearly.
DETROW: Fast-forward to now. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has spent the past week reminding the world of the importance of international support in interviews with American outlets...

PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: When Putin attacked us and began occupation, we didn't run away. We stood strong on the side of Western partners, on the side of Europe, and, of course, on the side of the American people.
ZELENSKYY: We're losing people and time. And it's a pity, because our children don't have see - don't have real-life childhood.

DETROW: ...And with members of Congress. Still, under President Trump, U.S. policy has taken a dramatic turn toward Russia. Paperwork to transfer critical munitions to Ukraine sits on the defense secretary's desk unsigned. Trump waived sanctions on Russia recently and signed an oil deal with Moscow. To take stock of this moment, we have called former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, William Taylor. Ambassador, thank you for joining us.
WILLIAM TAYLOR: Scott, thanks for having me.

DETROW: You served under both the George W. Bush administration and the Obama administration. And before we get into the last few weeks, let's start with this. What was the biggest material change in terms of the U.S. view of Ukraine when President Trump came back into office?

TAYLOR: Well, Scott, you remind us that the Russians actually first invaded in 2014, when Obama was president. And then when they invaded in 2022, and Biden was president, there was outrage. So that unified - there was a unified response, not just within the United States, but also internationally. And that we are now losing.

DETROW: You know, we all remember that blow-up meeting between Trump and Zelenskyy in the Oval Office in February 2025 - early months of this new administration. I think a lot of people found it shocking, and a lot of people thought at that time, well, that might be it for Ukraine in terms of U.S. support. TAYLOR: ...Which is to say that we, the United States and this administration, has much less influence, much less say about what goes on in this war.

TAYLOR: I think it's unlikely. I think it's unlikely because the American people and the Congress have been very clear in terms of the support for Ukraine and opposition to Putin. TAYLOR: President Trump has been pretty clear that he wants to end this war, and that's a good thing. And he's put some effort into a negotiation, and that's a good thing. The problem has been that he has given gifts - carrots - to the Russians and seems to have shifted into a pro-Russian stance and an anti-Ukrainian stance. That is not going to end the war. President Trump is not going to succeed in ending this war if he puts his weight behind the Russians, because the Ukrainians will not stop, Scott. The Ukrainians can't stop. DETROW: I mean, is there - there is a line of thinking that's pretty present in politics, that you're aware of, that's saying this war has been going on for four years. So many lives have been lost. TAYLOR: The Ukrainians have a say. The Ukrainians know what it's like to live under the Russians. They know this argument better than anyone. They know how bad it is for them. Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity

EDMONTON, Alberta — Voters in oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, according to referendum results released Tuesday, delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney's push for national unity as U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and annexation threats rally Canadians around their country.

With more than 1.8 million votes counted and results reported from 84% of voting areas and locations, 75% of voters supported remaining in Canada, while 25% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.
The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.
"It's a great result for Canada that Albertans have chosen unity," Carney told reporters Tuesday before a Cabinet meeting in Ottawa.

Carney said that the roughly one-quarter of Albertans who voted to begin the separation process did not necessarily want independence, saying only a smaller "hard core" group may actually want to leave Canada.
Some voters said they supported another referendum to express frustration with Ottawa rather than a desire to leave Canada.
"The result is absolutely clear. It's a vast majority in favor of staying in Canada. And now is the time to work together for all Albertans and all Canadians," Carney said.

Carney said he spoke with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Tuesday morning about the referendum's results and greater federal-provincial cooperation, including immigration. He said their first priority was supporting victims and families affected by the deadly military training fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.
Alberta's separatists, however, saw a silver lining.
"It is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better," said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.
Smith welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada.
"Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada," Smith posted on social media.

Smith, who called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, or UCP, despite opposing independence, said that she would address the province Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta's future.
"We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast," Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.
The results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday.
A fringe cause has become a movement that won't disappear

Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada's federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn't traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.
Despite the overwhelming rejection, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that won't disappear.

Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said.
Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.
At a separatist referendum night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell quiet as results rolled in.

"We're not going anywhere," said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. "We've dominated the conversation in the last year. We've been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we're going to continue moving forward."
Rath had said he would be thrilled with 30% support. He wants Smith ousted as UCP leader and said the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party.

Ian Brodie, a prominent conservative and political scientist at the University of Calgary who served as chief of staff to former prime minister Stephen Harper, dismissed current independence organizers Rath and Mitch Sylvestre as "nobodies."
"Even on a very soft question — whether to hold a referendum on separation — they couldn't gain real traction in the Olds-Didsbury district," said Brodie.
The district elected a Western Canada Concept separatist in a 1982 provincial byelection.
Edmonton voter Shawn Campbell said he voted to begin the separation process even though he doesn't want Alberta to leave Canada.
"It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy," he said.
Dustin Degenhardt, a voter in the town of Wainwright, said that Albertans have long been mistreated by Canada's federal government.
"Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony," he said after voting Monday. "They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything."
Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a "referendum on a referendum" rather than health care.
With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, "It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united. Instead we're fighting among ourselves."
Italy has approved the deployment of troops and tougher legal penalties in a bid to quell cost-of-living protests in the north of the country that occasionally turned violent over the weekend.

The Italian cabinet on Tuesday approved sending 500 troops to Milan, a new legal offence covering violent participation in a demonstration, tougher penalties for rioters and financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
Italy’s Ministry of Defence said the military will help reinforce security at key sites, step up surveillance of sensitive locations and enhance monitoring.

Unrest swept northern Italian cities at the weekend, including the financial capital Milan, where groups of mainly young people looted shops, smashed windows and clashed with the police. The demonstrations were driven by anger over soaring fuel and energy prices, high rents, low wages and the state of public services.

As part of the new legal measures, which take effect immediately, anyone who takes part in a group of at least five people and endangers public safety during protests faces up to five years in prison and a maximum fine of €20,000 ($22,460).
Penalties increase if faces are concealed or people are injured.
Authorities can order prompt compensation for any damage inflicted and, in the case of minors, hold their parents liable.

Police will be allowed to detain youths aged between 14 and 17, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence they pose a danger, extending powers that previously applied only to adults.
But the cabinet did not approve giving soldiers policing powers, as expected, after opposition from President Sergio Mattarella, Italian media reported.
“Destroying and stealing is not protest, it is crime, and the state’s response must be firm,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said in a social media post after the cabinet meeting.
The disturbances in northern Italy echoed riots in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent turmoil in years.

Meloni’s government is also facing mounting pressure from a separate wave of protests in southern Italy, where truck drivers angered by soaring diesel prices and the rising cost of living have staged roadblocks that are disrupting supply chains.
Protesters in both the north and the south say rising prices are pushing families into poverty, a concern for Meloni ahead of the 2027 national elections.
Elon Musk has revealed that SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a possible merger, a tie-up that would create a corporate colossus worth more than $3 trillion.
Musk said on Tuesday that his two largest companies had established special committees to explore a merger.
The SpaceX and Tesla CEO said the idea had a “lot of merit”, given the companies’ complementary work on artificial intelligence, but the committees had not come to any agreement on a proposal.
“They’ve got to come up with something, and then that’s got to be put to the shareholders as a vote,” Musk said on a SpaceX earnings call.
Musk, the world’s richest man with a net worth of more than $900bn, said that a merger would need to clear the “high hurdle” of a 50 percent vote among Tesla shareholders
“Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” Musk said.
“Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes. But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.”
A SpaceX-Tesla merger would rank as the biggest corporate tie-up in history, far exceeding the $1.25 trillion union between SpaceX and xAI in February.
At current valuations, SpaceX and Tesla rank as the world’s seventh- and eleventh-largest companies, respectively, with a combined market capitalisation of about $3.5 trillion.
Jerayr Haleblian, an expert in mergers and acquisitions at the University of California, Riverside, said a SpaceX-Tesla merger has “sound logic” to support it.

“In some sense, the core of both businesses are expert manufacturing. From a technology transfer perspective, there should be significant flows of information between businesses,” Haleblian told Al Jazeera.
“Both firms seem to have expertise in robotics, AI, energy infrastructure,” he said.
“Accordingly, the core skills are applicable across industry sectors. The key to success will be synergistic innovation, which I anticipate will follow from acquisition.”
Shares of SpaceX, which went public in June in the largest Initial Public Offering (IPO) of all time, rose more than 8 percent in after-hours trading following Musk’s comments.
Musk’s comments came as SpaceX on Tuesday reported its first quarterly profit, driven by strong growth in its AI and satellite-internet divisions.
Net profit was $4.4bn in the July-September quarter, a reversal from a $1.05bn net loss a year earlier.
Profit in the first three quarters totalled $413m, versus a loss of $2.59bn during the same period a year earlier.

Faecal bacteria are contaminating water in wells and sinkholes in Mexico’s Yucatan state, which are a vital source of drinking water, according to a report by Greenpeace, a global environmental organisation.
The report, published on Tuesday, said nearby pig farms and municipal wastewater were likely sources of the pollution in the southeastern coastal state.
“A range of chemical and microbiological indicators reveal a complex mosaic of severe, localised organic pollution,” it said.
Greenpeace called for an immediate moratorium on new industrial livestock operations and farm expansions in the peninsular state, which was once home to the ancient Maya civilisation.
With no above-ground rivers, groundwater is the Yucatan’s only freshwater source, and the area’s porous limestone bedrock lets pollutants quickly seep into the aquifer.
The global environmental watchdog group commissioned an independent laboratory to test water at 17 sites near the state capital, Merida, in August.
The sites included household and farm wells, community water points and cenotes, the natural sinkholes that dot the Yucatan Peninsula, which is one of Mexico’s most popular tourist destinations.

According to the report, every sample showed some degree of contamination likely linked to faecal waste, and several sites appeared heavily polluted. Total coliform bacteria reached the test’s upper limit in 16 of 17 samples, and faecal coliforms did so in 13.
However, the tests cannot show whether the waste came from people or animals, and leaking septic tanks and municipal sewage may also contribute to contamination.

Greenpeace said, however, that separate testing using Pig2Bac, a pig-specific DNA marker method, detected pig faecal matter in samples analysed at laboratories at Johns Hopkins University in the US and Mexico’s National Autonomous University (UNAM).
Greenpeace said the results raise “critical accountability questions” about nearby pig farms.
Maya communities joined Greenpeace in demanding action from environmental authorities over the contamination.

A UN report published in July found that there are more than 500 industrial pig farms across Yucatan state with more than 50,000 animals, many located near the lands and territories of Indigenous Peoples.

Marcos Orellana, a former UN special rapporteur who authored the report, said waste and chemicals from industrial farms “find their way very quickly” into the water communities use for bathing, cooking and drinking. He said most farms lack required permits and that regional government initiatives “remain insufficient”.
“The contamination of the waters that have sustained Mayan culture for millennia is predominantly coming from the industrial operations of the growth of animals,” Orellana said.

But Antonio Zumarraga, vice president of the Yucatan Citizen Scientific Water Observatory, defended the local pork industry, saying the sector has invested in water treatment and supports conservation programmes. He blamed local authorities for their inaction.
“It’s an issue that, as long as it doesn’t carry political weight for the government, they won’t do anything about it,” Zumarraga said.

The Yucatan state government was not available for comment, while Mexico’s national water commission, CONAGUA, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Merida’s Association of Pig Farmers also did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Thousands of people rallied in Lisbon, Porto and other Portuguese cities on Tuesday evening, hours after police dismantled protest camps and arrested a total of 55 demonstrators.
The protesters vowed to continue their campaign against Portugal's deepening housing crisis, which has made buying or renting a home increasingly unaffordable.
Organizers said more than 1,000 people gathered in each of the two main protest locations, although police did not provide crowd estimates.
In Lisbon's central Rossio square, demonstrators voted by a show of hands to re-establish their tent camp on Wednesday.
Police launched coordinated operations in Lisbon and Porto shortly before 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Tuesday, after warning protesters that their camps were illegal.
Activists had occupied Lisbon's Rossio square since Saturday, setting up around 200 tents. In Porto, protesters had camped in Dom Joao I square for about 10 days.
Authorities seized 228 camping structures during the operation.
In Porto, demonstrators dismantled their tents themselves after police threatened to intervene. In Lisbon, officers cleared the square as protesters formed a human chain.
Clashes subsequently broke out, according to footage broadcast by local television stations.
Carla Valadao, a spokesperson for the Lisbon camp, described the operation as "very aggressive."
However, Public Security Police superintendent Sergio Soares disputed that account, saying the eviction had been "calm, proportionate and appropriate, with no police charge."
All 55 people arrested were later released pending a court appearance in Lisbon on Wednesday.
Portugal is struggling with one of Europe's worst housing affordability crises.
Property purchase prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have nearly doubled over the same period.
The problem is particularly severe in major cities such as Lisbon and Porto, where residents have also protested against excessive tourism and an influx of so-called digital nomads.
Demonstrators accuse the center-right government of failing to address the crisis.
They are demanding the withdrawal of a bill that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The proposed legislation has already passed its first parliamentary reading.
Debora Miranda, a 41-year-old communications consultant, told Reuters she joined the Lisbon demonstration to represent generations struggling with rising housing costs.
"If people don't feel at home, in every sense of the word, they can't move forward with their lives...enough is enough."
Jorge Paixao, a 19-year-old history student, described the situation as "a societal crisis."
He said his generation needed "the ability to live with dignity, start families and rejuvenate Portugal."
Portugal housing protest takes place amid demos around Europe
The demonstrations come amid growing anger over housing affordability and living costs across several European countries.
Protesters in Portugal have sought to align their movement with similar demonstrations in neighboring Spain.
In Madrid, activists maintain a tent camp to call for stronger action to tackle the housing crisis. The crisis was sparked by the eviction ofMaria del Carmen Abascal from her home.
The nearly four weeks of protests in Spain have contributed to political turmoil, leading to a snap general election being called for November 29.
Meanwhile, demonstrations over rising living costs have also taken place in France, Belgium and Italy.

Violence that erupted in France over the weekend on the sidelines of otherwise peaceful protests has raised concerns that similar unrest could spread to other countries facing comparable economic pressures.

Nigeria's Health Ministry on Tuesday confirmed that the country had recorded its first known case of Ebola in the current outbreak. A woman who recently arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

The outbreak is thought to have started in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, not far from the Ugandan border, with Uganda the second country to record infections. It also recently spread to Kenya in limited numbers, with nine known cases recorded this month.
The overwhelming majority of known cases, however, remain confined to the DRC, particularly its eastern provinces.
What do we know about the Nigerian case of Ebola?
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said that the patient was a woman who had "recently arrived on an international flight from Uganda."

She first began to exhibit symptoms on October 7, and was admitted to a private Abuja hospital on October 11, before being tested and diagnosed with Ebola. He said authorities had already begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient.
"We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all contacts the individual may have had," he said.

Nigeria's Center for Disease Control said two weeks ago that it was stepping up surveillance after the first recorded cases in Kenya, saying it was improving the country's preparedness for a possible outbreak.

"These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of healthcare workers," the agency said.
Nigeria created an Ebola task force in June.

"We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat."
Over 9,000 cases in current outbreak, the fastest-growing on record
While Ebola does not spread as readily as highly contagious viruses like the flu or COVID, it is considerably more dangerous to those who do contract it.
The current outbreak, involving a lesser-known strain, the Bundibugyo Ebolavirus, has led to more than 9,000 confirmed cases and more than 4,300 deaths, a fatality rate of almost 50%.

Almost all the cases and deaths are confined to the DRC, even as more countries become involved. The first patient in Kenya died, and authorities believe the other eight known cases are all part of a cluster beginning with him. They say there's no sign of a spread beyond his contacts.

Uganda, which borders the Ituri province outbreak epicenter in DRC, reported 20 cases and two deaths quite much earlier this year. It was then declared Ebola-free in late August by the World Health Organization after reaching 42 days since a confirmed case. Tuesday's case in Nigeria could potentially put this status back into question, given the Health Ministry's comments on the patient's travel history.
This year's outbreak is already the second-largest on record and by far the fastest-spreading — although modestly improved testing and diagnostic capacity may also contribute to the higher numbers.

The West African Ebola epidemic of 2014-16 led to around 11,300 deaths from around 28,500 cases — but that was over a span of around 30 months. This outbreak was first declared in May of this year, although researchers believe it likely began in small numbers of cases several months earlier.
Guatemalan man gets 30 years for part in smuggling tragedy that killed 53 people in Texas
The 2022 incident was one of the deadliest human smuggling attempts along the U.S.-Mexico border

A U.S. federal judge on Tuesday sentenced a Guatemalan man extradited to the U.S. over his role in a 2022 human smuggling attempt that ended in the deaths of 53 migrants who had been transported in a sweltering tractor-trailer in Texas.

U.S. and Guatemalan prosecutors called Rigoberto Ramon Miranda Orozco's sentencing another step toward justice in one of the deadliest smuggling attempts along the U.S.-Mexico border. Miranda Orozco, 50, was sentenced to 30 years in prison after admitting to arranging travel and accommodations for two people who died and another who was seriously injured.

Nearly 20 people in the U.S. and Guatemala have been convicted since the discovery of the abandoned trailer full of bodies horrified communities accustomed to seeing their young people leave, trying to flee poverty or violence in Central America and Mexico.
"It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth," U.S. Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a news conference following the sentencing.

Police and other first responders work the scene where officials say dozens of people have been found dead and multiple others were taken to hospitals with heat-related illnesses after a semitrailer containing suspected migrants was found, June 27, 2022, in San Antonio, Texas. (Eric Gay/The Associated Press)

The trailer's air conditioning malfunctioned and would not blow cool air to the people trapped inside during the sweltering, three-hour ride in June 2022 from the border city of Laredo to San Antonio, authorities said. Prosecutors have said migrants paid up to $15,000 US each to be taken across the U.S. border.
When the abandoned trailer was opened on a remote San Antonio back road, 48 migrants were dead. Another 16 were taken to hospitals, where five more died.

Simmons said investigators found clothing passengers had shed to cool off and claw marks on the trailer's walls.
"They were literally trying to claw their way out," he said.
Twenty-one of those who died were from Guatemala, Simmons said.

Rigoberto Ramon Miranda Orozco, seen here in September 2024, was sentenced to 30 years in prison Tuesday for his role in the 2022 human smuggling case that left 53 migrants dead. (Moises Castillo/The Associated Press)

Miranda Orozco's attorney, Alfonso Cabanas Jr., called the sentence "very tough." He said his client was in Guatemala at the time and had no control over the type of transportation the migrants would take to San Antonio nor did he know the air conditioning was malfunctioning.
Cabanas said he doesn't think harsh punishments will "make a dent" in such operations.
"What we do need is comprehensive immigration reform," Cabanas said.
U.S. District Judge Orlando Garcia sentenced Miranda Orozco, who was arrested in Guatemala in 2024 and extradited to the U.S. the following year.

He pleaded guilty in July to conspiracy to bring a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in serious bodily injury, prosecutors said.

Simmons said prosecutors in Guatemala were integral in securing convictions for Miranda Orozco and others. Simmons was joined by Guatemalan Attorney General Gabriel García Luna, who reflected on the suffering the migrants inside the tractor-trailer endured.
"They paid for a promise, and those who cashed in on that promise abandoned them to their fate," García Luna said.

Last year, Felipe Orduna-Torres, described by prosecutors as the leader of the smuggling operations inside the U.S., was sentenced to life in prison in the U.S. Armando Gonzales-Ortega, his top assistant, was sentenced to 83 years.

The tragedy is the deadliest among those that have claimed thousands of lives in recent decades as people attempt to cross the U.S. border from Mexico. Ten migrants died in 2017 after they were trapped inside a truck parked at a Walmart in San Antonio.
In 2003, the bodies of 19 migrants were found in a sweltering truck southeast of San Antonio.
NFL players' union wants investigation of how Jalen Hurts's blood clots were handled
League staunchly defends Philadelphia Eagles franchise's handling of situation
The NFL staunchly defended the Philadelphia Eagles' handling of quarterback Jalen Hurts's blood clots on Tuesday, while hours later the players' union called for an investigation of the situation.

A person with knowledge of the situation confirmed to The Associated Press that the Eagles were not being disciplined for their actions with Hurts. The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because conversations between the league and team were to remain private.

Dr. Allen Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer, offered a passionate defence of how the Eagles treated Hurts, following a statement from the league that said officials had been in contact with Philadelphia's medical personnel and the Cleveland Clinic in London, England, throughout the process.

"I have complete confidence in the Eagles' medical staff and their handling of this situation, and I would characterize their work as very conservative, very patient-focused and appropriately guarded at every step," Sills said at the league's annual fall meeting.

"I don't think you can take that outcome and say there was something flawed about the process. Sometimes in medicine, we do all the right things and diseases progress and other things develop ... in this case, everyone was incredibly conservative and incredibly vigilant and was very quick to make diagnoses of these conditions that might not have been diagnosed in a non-athlete."
The NFL Players Association in a statement said it was told by the league that a review was not planned.

"Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred," the union said. "Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward."

Hurts is on injured reserve and expected to miss the rest of the season after a blood clot in his left calf travelled to his lungs. The Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said Monday that Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary embolisms.
NFL executive vice president Jeff Miller took issue with "uninformed speculation" in reports Monday that Hurts went more than 30 hours without sleep last weekend before playing.
"Jalen Hurts returned to the hotel, slept for a period of time and went to the stadium," Miller said, estimating that Hurts slept for around seven or eight hours.

"Both talking to the Eagles' staff and making sure from people on the ground, tracking the case, talking to the independent hospital and doctors involved that we have, I think, a complete understanding of the course of events."

Sills said the league and the players' union study and track blood clots annually. He declined to go into specifics about Hurts's condition, citing patient privacy, and reiterated multiple times that treating a blood clot involves looking at multiple factors.
Dr. Caron Rockman, a vascular surgeon for roughly 30 years, said based on what she has read, there's no evidence the Eagles acted improperly while dealing with what she called not a textbook issue.

"It's a judgment call," said Rockman, who is currently a chair at Hackensack University Medical Center in New Jersey and did not treat Hurts. "I think it's really a case-by-case basis. In my personal opinion, superficial vein thrombosis is not a [disqualification] to fly."
Hurts's treatment moving forward involves blood thinners, and he will not be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them.

"I think there was incredible vigilance, there was conservative care, state-of-the-art imaging that was done in London," Sills said. "And, as far as the timing and the decision-making, I have great confidence in that and believe that everyone acted with an abundance of caution."
Sills, in his opening statement that lasted more than five minutes, said all decisions are made with medicine over football.
"The notion that there are external factors or that any of our physicians would put a player in harm's way — that's nonsense," Sills said.
Trump walks back threat to ban Bombardier sales in the U.S.

U.S. President Donald Trump has backed down on a threat to ban Bombardier plane sales in the United States, allowing the aerospace sector to breathe a sigh of relief after tempers flared and tariffs rose in an escalation of the trade war last month.
Speaking at a campaign rally Monday night, Trump said he's changed his perception of the Montreal-based business jet maker as a purely Canadian manufacturer.
"I'm going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away," he told a crowd in a suburb of Wichita, Kan., where Bombardier employs 1,500 workers.

"I always viewed them as a Canadian company ... but now I find out they have a presence here, and we're not hurting them if they're in Kansas. So we'll take care of those people, all right? And the jobs."
Wichita serves as the home base of Bombardier's defence division. The company employs about 3,500 American workers across plants in Kansas, Texas, California and other states.
Republican stronghold Kansas now a battleground

Kansans are already feeling first-hand the effects of the president's policies. Midwestern farmers have seen the diesel that powers their tractors and combines rise to near-record prices due to the Iran war. Kansas has now turned into a political battleground as Republicans and Democrats fight for control of the typically red state ahead of next month's midterm elections.

Trump said Monday that a phone call from Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall helped convince him to walk back his threat against Bombardier. Polls show Marshall is running neck and neck with Adam Hamilton, a Democrat in a state that has not elected one to the Senate since 1932.

Last month, Trump suggested he would bar Bombardier aircraft sales in the United States unless it moved its operations there, despite the harm experts said such a move would inflict on American workers.
"NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" he posted on social media on Sept. 7. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank."'
Bombardier responded that it pays more than $2.5 billion US to some 2,800 American suppliers across 47 states each year, indirectly supporting tens of thousands of jobs.
"The American aerospace industry is a clear winner on trade and exports," Bombardier stated in September, adopting the language of the president and his fixation on triumph and trade surpluses.
Last week, the company inaugurated a skills development centre for new aircraft technicians and mechanics in Wichita, part of a $50-million US investment in the site.

"Our recently announced investments and newly inaugurated North American Learning Center will support high-skilled jobs for many years to come," a spokesperson for Bombardier said Tuesday in a statement to CBC News. "We are proud of our engaged workforce in Wichita as well as in all 20-plus states [where] Bombardier employs team members."
America enjoys a $109-billion US aerospace and defence trade surplus with the world, according to the U.S. Aerospace Industries Association.
Bombardier does the final assembly of its Challenger and Global business jets in Canada, while more than half of its revenue stems from American customers.

"We view the removal of this regulatory uncertainty as positive for sentiment as it alleviates an important headline overhang for investors," said James McGarragle, an analyst at RBC Dominion Securities.
Trump's threat did not have a "tangible impact" on demand for the luxury jets among American customers over the past six weeks, he added.
Bombardier shares rose $13.85 US or about 4.5 per cent to close at $325.32 US on Tuesday.
Despite U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and other goods, aerospace manufacturing remains deeply integrated across the continent and beyond.
Most Bombardier planes feature at least 40 per cent U.S. content, analysts say. More than half of the value of the ultra-long-range Global 7500 luxury jet derives from American parts.
Blocking a major manufacturer from the market would "undoubtedly" cause revenue and job losses at American parts producers, said National Bank analyst Cameron Doerksen last month.
A ban would have also been "massively disruptive" to the many American jet fleet operators awaiting Bombardier deliveries, he said.
Trump's fist-shaking went down a day before Ottawa's retaliatory tariffs on American goods took effect on Sept. 8, a response to the 50 per cent duties Washington imposed on Canadian goods in August.
Trump then proceeded to ban most Canadian alcoholic drinks, some dairy products and motorcycles, among other products, and slapped a 50 per cent levy on more items.
Trump's September Truth Social post marked the second time this year Bombardier has come into the president's crosshairs.

In January, he singled out Bombardier in a threat to ground all Canadian-made aircraft and slap them with a 50 per cent tariff unless Ottawa approved Gulfstream business jets — assembled in Savannah, Ga. — marking an earlier escalation of trade tensions between the two countries.
Bass Coast Shire Council has rejected a bid by McDonald's to open a restaurant on Phillip Island.
The application drew an angry response from members of the Phillip Island community.
McDonald's can appeal the decision to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal.
An application by McDonald's to build a restaurant in the Victorian tourist hotspot of Phillip Island has been rejected after councillors voted to refuse it a planning permit.
The fast-food giant lodged its application earlier this year with the Bass Coast Shire Council to build a new restaurant in Cowes, which has a population of 6,593.

Island ward councillor Tim O'Brien said the proposal failed the community "on so many levels".
"Where is the community benefit?" Mr O'Brien said.
"This will be muscling its way into a part of a market it had no part in building."
Councillor Mat Morgan, who is a Greens candidate at the upcoming Victorian election, said the application "should obviously be rejected" because of inappropriate residential development.
"There are a thousand ethical and moral reasons to throw this in the bin," he said.
"We don't want this, we don't need this."
The proposal raised the ire of thousands of residents, with more than 5,800 people signing a petition rejecting the proposal, citing traffic concerns and the threat to small businesses in town.
The no vote came after a recommendation by council officers to grant McDonald's a planning permit, which they found "acceptable" after assessing it against the planning scheme.

The council received 1,543 objections and 32 submissions relating to the McDonald's application.
The proposed site is home to a petrol station and a vacant plot of land.
Cowes resident and business owner, Trevor Ware, said the community's concerns were heard by the council in rejecting the proposal.
"We didn't need this and I think the community has done very well to fight it," he said.
