The trial of a Cairns teenager who detained a man at knifepoint while his partner was being raped has concluded after three days of evidence.
The case hinged on whether the then-16-year-old knew his co-offenders intended to rape the woman.
The judge has retired to consider his verdict.
A judge has retired to consider whether a teenager who held a man at knifepoint during a Cairns home invasion is also guilty of raping the man's partner.

The judge-only, three-day trial in the Childrens Court of Queensland, sitting in Cairns, hinged on one question: whether the boy heard a co-offender tell the woman he intended to sexually assault her.
The defendants and victims cannot be identified for legal reasons.
Evidence heard in closed court by Judge Joshua Treviño KC included pre-recorded evidence from the couple and the boy, as well as evidence from police.
The teenager was one of three boys who broke into a home in the Cairns suburb of Manunda about 3am on February 21 last year.
The couple were woken by burglars in their bedroom.
The court heard while the defendant held the man at knifepoint, his two co-accused took the woman to other parts of the house and raped her multiple times.
The two co-accused have pleaded guilty to rape, and their cases remain before the courts.
The defendant has pleaded guilty to six charges, including stealing, going armed in company and detaining the couple in their home, but has pleaded not guilty to five counts of rape.
Yesterday, the court was shown the boy's police interview after his arrest, in which he appeared shocked when Detective Senior Constable Damon Smalley told him the details of the rape.
"I did not know anything about that. I was in the room with the other person and holding him in the room," the boy said.
When Senior Constable Smalley, from the Police Child Protection and Investigation Unit, asked whether he had at any point tried to stop anything happening to the woman, the boy replied: "No."
Defence barrister Timothy Grau argued his client never intended to be involved in a sexual assault and instead believed his co-offenders were only robbing the woman.
He told the court the boy either did not hear or did not understand what one of his co-accused said about the woman before she was led from the bedroom.
"At that point, that she's being removed from the bedroom to leave the room, at that point the conversation, it's about [stealing] wallets and money," Mr Grau said.
"So, the purpose of his detention … is a robbery."
The court also heard the boy believed he would be stabbed by his co-accused if he did not detain the man.
Crown prosecutor Nicole Friedewald told the court her case relied on the evidence of the woman's partner.
She said the man heard one of the co-accused say he intended to sexually assault the woman as she was led from the bedroom at knifepoint to get her wallet.
The court heard the boy was told to get a knife from the kitchen and hold the man in the room.
"The suggestion he did not hear that statement … and did not respond to it, as [the man] has given evidence, defies logic and belief," Ms Friedewald said.
The trial included lengthy exchanges between the judge, prosecution and defence over how the rape charge would or would not apply to someone who had no physical contact with the victim.
Ms Friedewald argued the boy was criminally responsible under Section 7 of the Queensland Criminal Code, because he aided and enabled the rapes by keeping the woman's partner from stopping them.
"He was, in those circumstances, the only person who could have intervened, who could have protected that complainant, and he was prevented by this defendant from doing so," she said.
Her alternative argument relied on Section 8 of the code, which says those who share a common intention to carry out an unlawful purpose can be held responsible for offences committed along the way.

She also pointed to provisions of the Evidence Act 1977, recognising that people involved in non-consensual sexual activity may give differing accounts and respond in different ways, and that victims do not need to have been physically injured or threatened.
Judge Treviño told the court he intended to reach a decision as soon as possible.
The Queensland government added rape to its adult crime, adult time reforms three months after the offending alleged in this case took place.
An inquest into the death of Elizabeth Struhs has heard child safety workers failed to recognise significant coercive control being exercised on her father, Jason Struhs.
Jason Struhs, Elizabeth's mother Kerrie Struhs, and eleven others were found guilty of manslaughter after withholding her insulin for type 1 diabetes in 2022.

Child safety workers failed to recognise the significant coercive control that Elizabeth Struhs's mother and fringe church group were subjecting on her father when assessing the eight-year-old's future risk of harm, an inquest has heard.
Elizabeth Struhs's body was found at her Toowoomba home in January 2022 after her father Jason Struhs stopped providing her insulin for her type 1 diabetes.
He had recently converted to a sect named The Saints, which his wife Kerrie Struhs was a member of.
The group holds anti-medical intervention views and instead believed that God would save Elizabeth.
An inquest probing various government agencies' involvement in the case has so far run for a week and a half and heard from more than 20 witnesses.
Today a child safety worker gave evidence about various mistakes she said were made in Elizabeth's initial risk assessment and resulting case plan.
"Child safety were too narrowly focused on Elizabeth's diabetes management and failed to identify the power imbalance of Mr and Mrs Struhs," she said.

According to the child safety witness, staff "failed to identify the serious risk of harm Mrs Struhs's beliefs surrounding medical intervention could have had on Elizabeth", as well as the presence of domestic and family violence.
She said the case plan identified just one form of abuse, when there were two.
"Exposure to domestic and family violence in terms of coercive control," she said.
The woman said if staff had recognised that factor they would have looked at other ways to support Jason Struhs.

"To withstand the coercive control, if possible, that was occurring in relation to the importance of the religious beliefs of Mrs Struhs and their older children which then weighed heavily on Jason," she said.

The Brisbane Corconer's Court heard on Friday, Elizabeth risk of future neglect should have also been flagged at various stages, including when Mrs Struhs was questioned by a doctor and two child safety workers.
The child safety worker said, while every person has a right to their own beliefs, they must still, by law, ensure a child's protection and safety.

In mid-2019 Elizabeth was taken to hospital in a comatose state by her father against her mother's wishes, which is when the Child Safety Department became involved, and required the couple to sign an intervention with parental agreement (IPA) which stipulated Mr Struhs would continue providing Elizabeth with her lifesaving medicine, and that Kerrie Struhs wouldn't intervene.
In 2021 Kerrie Struhs spent several months in jail over the incident.

It was at this stage, the inquest heard, that her husband converted to the sect, falling "into their hold, coercive control and belief system", which was a "very significant event in terms of what caused or contributed to Elizabeth's death".
Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris questioned the child safety worker over whether the department should have intervened when Kerrie Struhs was first sent to jail.

She said that fact would have been viewed as a positive that would have reduced Elizabeth's risk rather than increased it, and pointed to Jason Struhs's swift conversion to the sect as a major complicating factor.
"It would have been very hard to predict."
In 2025 Mr and Mrs Struhs were each sentenced to 14 years for their daughter's manslaughter, after first being acquitted of murder.
Eleven other members of The Saints were sentenced to between six and nine years in prison for their involvement.

From accessing their money to ordering a taxi or takeout, millions of Russians were feeling the impact of Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of the country’s internet giant Yandex in their daily life.

“I ended up in a situation where I had absolutely no money. Well, I had the money, but it was inaccessible,” said Irina, a blogger from St. Petersburg, who had not been able to access her money for four days when she spoke with NBC News last week.

Irina, who like several other people did not want her last name shared while she was speaking with a foreign news organization about a sensitive matter, said her rent was due the day the first outages happened, when she hoped “that it would be fixed in a few hours.” Days later, she still had no access to money to pay for utilities or even food for her small child.
The strikes that took place over several days this month were the first publicized attacks on Russian data centers as Ukraine seeks to bring the war home for Russians.

The disruption hit myriad services provided by Yandex, a tech giant akin to Google whose services are deeply integrated into daily life in Russia and whose digital infrastructure other third-party platforms rely on.

Many people took to social media to complain about not being able to order taxis or food delivery. Others reported not being able to access their files on the company’s storage service, while some even struggled to get into their homes after their digital keys went offline.

While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.
Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.
Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that it is working to restore service.
“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”

Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between Moscow and the southern city of Krasnodar, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.

“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has 2 million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before.”

Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.
She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them. This came from the outside.”

Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, 30, a barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after she was unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.
She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay but that the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.

Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they could not see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He is originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.

Another driver, Valery from Krasnodar, had been on the job for only a few months, having previously worked at a packing center for Wildberries, Russia’s retail giant, whose warehouse was attacked by Ukrainian drones in July.
When the Yandex outages started, he said, the taxi app would show error messages or even send several cars for the same customer.

While that has been largely resolved, said Valery, 24, the biggest issue for him was that he could not withdraw the money that he had already earned with Yandex. “If I can’t access my pay in another week or two, I will start looking for another job,” he said.
In addition to Yandex, the data centers of Russia’s biggest bank, Sberbank, and the tech giant VK have also been targeted in recent days.

The chaos is no accident, analysts say. “Ukraine’s campaign from the start has had as one of its objectives bringing home to ordinary Russians the fact that they are at war and this involves consequences,” Keir Giles, an associate fellow at Chatham House, a British think tank, told NBC News.
The aim, Giles said, is for everyday Russians to conclude that their lives are being disrupted because of their leaders’ actions in waging war.
Yandex may also be a target because of its role in shaping what Russians see online, said Robert Tollast, a drone expert and researcher at the Royal United Services Institute in London.
Data centers also have growing military value, Tollast said, as both sides use battlefield data to improve operations and commanders’ situational awareness, potentially with AI-assisted planning.

Asked about the outages and whether the government was looking into financially assisting those affected, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was premature to talk about government support, because Yandex is “facing difficulties,” but it is “strong and powerful.” Meanwhile, Russian authorities were looking at protecting data centers after the “unprecedented attack,” Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said.
On Wednesday, President Vladimir Putin held a meeting on enhancing the level of digital security in Russia, but Peskov said it was not linked to the attacks on data centers.

Russia has increasingly ramped up its own attacks on Ukrainian data centers, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accusing Moscow of trying to “leave Ukrainians without the internet.” Ukraine was reciprocating those strikes by hitting Yandex, he said in a speech last week, adding without providing evidence that “it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms” because there were fewer Russian bots around. NBC News could not verify whether Yandex services’ going down had that effect.
While both sides have hit data centers, Russia’s were easier targets, said Mykhailo Samus, a Ukrainian military analyst and director of the New Geopolitics Research Network.

While Ukraine’s data centers are widely dispersed, many of Russia’s are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, he said, meaning a strike on a single site can disrupt services spanning transportation, internet access and payments.
“Very easy and very important,” he said.
Christian Horner reveals Red Bull talks with Lewis Hamilton management before telling Mercedes' Niki Lauda to sign British driver

Christian Horner joins Simon Lazenby on the latest episode of Sky Sports' The F1 Show Podcast to reveal all on Red Bull talks with Lewis Hamilton before the latter joined Mercedes and his thoughts on Kimi Antonelli, who could become world champion this Sunday at the United States GP
Christian Horner has revealed he helped Mercedes sign Lewis Hamilton after holding early discussions with the British driver's management to join Red Bull.
Hamilton left McLaren to join Mercedes at the start of 2013 but in Horner's new book, 'Drive ', which will be on sale from this Thursday, he says Hamilton showed interest to join Red Bull.
Senior figures at Red Bull, including co-owner Dietrich Mateschitz, were not keen on the move that would have seen Hamilton replace Mark Webber and become Sebastian Vettel's team-mate from 2013.
Vettel had won the last three drivers' titles at the time and Horner explained the situation on Sky Sports' The F1 Show Podcast.
"As a team principal, it's your job to understand what is the driver market. Naturally, when you've got the fastest car, the best drivers want to drive in the best cars," said Horner.
"It's only natural that Lewis was interested in that stage. We had a totally dominant car and he was managed at the time by Simon Fuller, who managed the Spice Girls.

"I remember Simon telling me that he and I could do the biggest sport deal that sport had ever seen, which would inevitably mean Red Bull paying a lot of money. There wasn't an enthusiasm to do that within the team. We had a winning driver in Seb, did we really need to upset the apple cart?"

Three-time F1 world champion Niki Lauda, who was Mercedes' non-executive chairman at the time of Hamilton's negotiations with other teams in the second half of 2012, is often credited for signing Hamilton to Mercedes for 2013.
But, Horner says he told Lauda to sign Hamilton after Red Bull decided to retain their driver line-up of Vettel and Webber.
"Mercedes, who had only just bought the Brawn team, was struggling. They had a few years with Nico [Rosberg] and Michael [Schumacher], and it wasn't really coming together there," he said.
"When Nikki turned up at Mercedes, it felt like, do you know what, why don't you go for Lews, who was inevitably becoming frustrated at McLaren? And Nikki persuaded him to go there.

"I remember, I think the crux time was around the Singapore Grand Prix [in September of] that year, where Lewis was in the lead, and he had a gearbox failure. That was sort of the nail in the coffin, I think, for McLaren.
"We won the race with Seb and I remember being on the podium and looking down, and Nikki was there. He took his hat off, which he rarely did, but then gave me the biggest thumbs up.
"I think things [negotiations] had sort of been happening over that weekend and he knew that result was only going to help his cause."
Horner: Fascinating if 'special talent' Antonelli goes head to head with Verstappen
Horner was sacked by Red Bull in July 2025 but has continued to watch Formula 1 from home and recently saw Max Verstappen win in Malaysia and Singapore.

Verstappen joined Red Bull from the fifth round of 2016, after just over a year in F1, and won his first race with the Milton Keynes-based outfit as an 18-year-old - and remains the youngest winner of a Grand Prix.
Horner says the victory was "fairy-tale stuff" and that Verstappen is the greatest talent he's seen.

"I think it was clear from very early on in his career and certainly Formula 1 career that this was somebody with an abnormal talent - so young, but driving like a veteran with such conviction, such authority and aggression," he said.

"His ability to get to the limit of what the car was capable of, his ability to have so much spare capacity, whilst doing that and understanding everything that was going on around him in the race with the car, tyres, you hardly had to tell him which control switches to make change to because he was already ahead of it himself.
"When he arrived with us, he was still quite inexperienced relative to others because he's only done one year in the lower formula.
"Some of his learning was done very publicly. His mental strength and aptitude and ability to deliver really high-pressure moments was something I certainly hadn't witnessed before."

Kimi Antonelli is set to break Vettel's record as F1's youngest world champion at 20 years old, with his first opportunity to wrap up the title coming this weekend at the United States Grand Prix in Austin.
This year is first time Verstappen has not been in a title fight since 2020 and Horner is looking forward to seeing Antonelli take on Verstappen in future seasons.

"It's still early days for Kimi. I think Kimi has done a phenomenal job this year. You can see the lessons he's learned from his rookie season applied this year. He's made a massive step and George Russell's no idiot, so to be getting on top of him is truly impressive," he said.

"What will be interesting is, he's going to win this championship at a canter, it'll be fascinating in future years if he does get the opportunity to go head to head with Max. I think that will be fascinating. But he is undoubtedly, again, another very special talent."

AI on track to ‘crowd out’ human decision-making in warfare

Artificial intelligence is already being widely used on the battlefield, and the role of human judgment in military operations is shrinking rapidly, the head of the UN’s independent disarmament research institute warned on Tuesday.

In a briefing at UN Headquarters in New York, UNIDIR Director Robin Geiss had a stark question for journalists: “Are we going to let machines target and kill human beings?” he asked, warning that AI was increasingly “on track to crowding out human decision-making” in the sector.
The UN Secretary General has been repeatedly urging stakeholders to make sure we do not cross this "moral red line."
AI is being given a growing number of responsibilities in military affairs, from intelligence analysis and target identification to drone operations and orchestrating cyber-attacks.
Crucially, this comes at the expense of human judgement, including in the nuclear domain, Mr. Geiss stressed.

The shift is dramatically increasing the pace of battlefield operations, shortening the time between identifying and striking targets and allowing forces to engage an unprecedented number of targets each day.
At the same time, many of these evolving AI systems are opaque, and the UNIDIR chief warned they are increasing the risk of error, miscalculation and therefore of unintended escalation.
As AI tools are becoming easier to use, it will also become easier for non-State actors to engage in ever-more sophisticated military operations, he said.
Mr. Geiss recognised that geopolitical competition and tensions are “serious obstacles” to regulating AI involvement in the military sector.
Yet he also stressed that concerns about its risks are increasingly being shared – regardless of political outlook – including among major global powers.

In September, for example, the United States proposed an AI “notification mechanism” with China, so the world’s two largest military spenders can warn each other about AI incidents that could threaten national security.

The UN Secretary General's repeated calls for stronger regulation of military AI and a legally binding treaty on lethal autonomous weapon systems are also “increasingly [finding] an echo across the international community,” the UNIDIR Director said.
The UNIDIR is working actively to create some of the building blocks required for multilateral cooperation on the matter.

On Thursday, the UNIDIR Centre of Excellence on AI, Peace and Security will launch a new multi-stakeholder forum on AI in international peace and security and in the military domain – the first and only such forum within the UN system so far, said Mr. Geiss.
1. Developing a framework for responsible industry behaviour, with practical, voluntary guidelines for companies to follow at the design and development stage for AI military tools.

2. Developing an “AI security lexicon” to clarify key concepts such as autonomy, safety or security, which are currently being used very differently by different stakeholders – creating ambiguity that hinders trust and cooperation.
3. Addressing the risk of misuse of AI by non-State armed groups to support operational planning, execution, and logistics.
As Sudan war spills into Central African Republic, UN warns against early peacekeeper exit

CAR continues to face a resurgence of deadly violence in the east despite the disarmament of nearly 2,000 fighters and the gradual completion of the latest electoral cycle, the Security Council heard.

Illustrating the current fragility, the top UN official in the country, Valentine Rugwabiza, highlighted an attack on 30 June by different armed groups on Am-Dafock, bordering Sudan, which killed civilians, members of national security forces, displaced 17,000 civilians and injured six UN peacekeepers.

However, without peacekeeping mission MINUSCA’s rapid response, she said, attacks in the border area with Chad and Sudan would have resulted in significantly more fatalities and State authority could not have been restored after only five days of control by the armed group, whose fighters retreated across the border into Sudan.

“In this regard, I plead with the council, as it prepares to renew MINUSCA’s mandate, to maintain MINUSCA with adequate force levels and capabilities during the critical consolidation phase,” she stressed.

While Bangui consolidates its authority and continues disarming rebel groups, violence is multiplying in the east, driven in part by the war in Sudan that is complicating plans for a gradual MINUSCA troop drawdown, Ms. Rugwabiza said.

The situation in the northeast and southeast remained particularly worrying, notably around mining sites and along the corridors traditionally used by pastoral farmers – often the source of community tensions.

In the southeast, 26 serious incidents were recorded, attributed to suspected members of the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA – a long-established armed group of Ugandan origin – between June and September.
They included reports of rapes and sexual slavery and the abduction of 68 civilians, around 40 of them children.
At the same time, the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) militia continues to threaten local populations.
However, Ms. Rugwabiza announced Monday’s release of three hostages held since December 2025, including the sub-prefect of Bambouti, following several months of mediation with local leaders.

This violence contrasts with advances in the peace process. Since July 2025, 1,907 fighters have been disarmed and demobilised, but their economic re-integration remains difficult and some cannot be located.

Politically, elections are ending. As of 1 October, 127 of the 177 municipalities had installed their municipal councils. The remaining polls, postponed for lack of financial and logistical resources, are due to be held on 25 October.

Yet, this institutional progress is not enough to improve living conditions. Nearly two million Central Africans, or 31 per cent of the population, faced acute food insecurity between April and August.
At the beginning of October, the UN humanitarian plan was only 46.6 per cent funded.

It is in this context that the Security Council must decide, before mid-November, whether to renew MINUSCA’s mandate. The mission has already closed several bases in regions deemed sufficiently stable and transferred certain responsibilities to national authorities.

MINUSCA was deployed in 2014, a year after Séléka, a predominantly Muslim coalition, seized power by force and overthrew then-President François Bozizé, triggering a spiral of violence, looting, massacres of civilians and sexual violence.
More than 10 years later, Séléka has been dissolved, two presidential elections have been held and a 2019 peace agreement has brought 14 armed groups into a political process.
Meanwhile, vast areas remain unstable. Right now, the UN peacekeeping mission maintains more than 12,000 peacekeepers.

According to Ms. Rugwabiza, initial assessments show no major deterioration in security in the localities affected by base closures. But, this reorganisation relies in particular on long-range patrols and on strengthening Central African forces.
The issue has divided Security Council members. The United States has already argued for larger troop reductions while other countries warn against a hasty withdrawal.
The UN Secretary-General recommended extending the mandate by one year while preserving the military capabilities needed for rapid intervention.

After more than a decade of MINUSCA’s presence, CAR has recovered some of its institutions and territory. However, the violence that persists at its borders is a reminder of how dependent these gains remain on international support.
Bangladesh: UNICEF chief calls for an end to child marriage

Her story was one of many heard by the UN children’s agency Executive Director Catherine Russell who on Tuesday called for urgent investment in Bangladesh’s children following a three-day visit to the country.

Ms. Russell urged action on three fronts: ending child marriage and keeping girls in school, delivering on the Government’s commitment to invest five per cent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) in both education and health, and protecting quality learning for Rohingya refugee and host-community children.
“Keeping girls in school and providing them with the health, education and protection services they need will deliver a brighter future for them, for their communities, and for Bangladesh,” she said.
In Korail, Dhaka’s largest informal settlement, Ms. Russell heard from children and parents how poverty, disrupted education and limited basic services have impacted their lives.
Adolescent girls shared their ambitions and the pressures that can force them out of school and into marriage.
Nearly half – 47.2 per cent – of women in Bangladesh aged 20 to 24 were married before the age of 18, according to the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025.

Child marriage drives girls out of school, fuels early pregnancy and narrows lifelong opportunities. UNICEF is calling for girls to complete secondary school and for loopholes in national law that permit child marriage to be closed.

Meeting senior officials, including State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam, Ms. Russell welcomed the Government’s commitment to increase spending on education and health, while stressing the importance of turning promises into action.
“Budgets reflect priorities,” she said. “Investing in children’s quality education, health, nutrition and protection is investing in Bangladesh’s future.”

In Cox’s Bazar, home to one of the largest refugee camps in the world, Ms. Russell met Rohingya children and families and visited a UNICEF-supported learning centre, where students and teachers spoke about the importance of education and vocational skills.
Beyond learning, education protects children from exploitation, trafficking, child marriage and recruitment by armed groups, UNICEF said.

“Rohingya children have lost so much to violence, displacement and uncertainty. They cannot lose their education too,” Ms. Russell said. “The world must invest in them, and in the communities that welcomed them.”

Recognizing Bangladesh’s generosity in hosting the refugees, she appealed to the international community to keep supporting both the Rohingya and their host communities, warning that as humanitarian funding declines, sustained support is critical to protect essential services.
In Cox’s Bazar, UNICEF and partners provide life-saving and essential services to Rohingya refugee children and families.
As humanitarian funding declines sustained international support is critical to protect essential services and ensure that refugee and host-community children are not left behind.

Hurricane Isaias—the only Atlantic hurricane to date in 2026—made landfall in Florida as a Category 2 storm on October 9. After delivering a rainy, windy blow to the U.S. Gulf Coast and drenching much of the Eastern Seaboard, the weather system had more in store.

Riding the jet stream east over the North Atlantic, Isaias’s remnants developed into a powerful storm known as an extratropical cyclone. These low-pressure systems often feature asymmetrical, comma-shaped cloud patterns and can strike with hurricane-force winds, rain, and blizzard-like conditions.

The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-21 satellite captured this image of the extratropical cyclone brushing past Iceland on the afternoon of October 14. During its journey, the system’s air pressure plummeted by more than 50 hectopascals over a 24-hour period, according to reports—approximately double the criteria for explosive cyclogenesis, or bombogenesis. Some meteorologists believe the storm may have set a new October low for barometric pressure in Iceland, after correcting for altitude, likely breaking a record that has stood since 1963.

The cyclone lashed Iceland with high winds as it grazed the coast. A gust of 205 kilometers (128 miles) per hour was recorded near Eyjafjallajökull volcano in the country’s south, while a small island just offshore saw sustained winds of 150 kilometers (93 miles) per hour. Damaging winds extended into northern parts of the country, where residents also braced for sleet and snow. Farther across the Atlantic, northwestern Scotland received gusts up to 90 kilometers (55 miles) per hour on October 14, according to news reports, resulting in cancellations on several ferry routes.

SpaceX will soon notch a huge spaceflight milestone, if all goes according to plan.

The company will try to catch both stages of its Starship megarocket during the vehicle's next test flight, which is targeted for next month, founder and CEO Elon Musk announced during SpaceX's quarter 3 (Q3) earnings call today (Oct. 20).

If SpaceX succeeds, this "will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered," Musk said. "The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle. So this is, I think, a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization and consciousness."
Starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall when fully stacked.

As Musk noted, both of its stages — the Super Heavy booster and Ship spacecraft — are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX thinks will make Mars settlement and other grand exploration feats economically feasible.

Starship's recovery strategy is different than that for SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets, which are partially reusable. (The latter two rockets have expendable upper stages). Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy boosters come back to Earth on landing pads near the launch site or on ships at sea downrange. Super Heavy and Ship, however, will steer themselves directly back to their launch tower, which will capture each vehicle with its "chopstick" arms.

This will allow SpaceX to inspect, refurbish and refly Starship at an accelerated rate, which is a priority for the company: Musk has said he envisions launching Starship more than 10,000 times per year by 2030.

Starship has conducted 14 test flights to date, and SpaceX has pulled off chopstick catches with Super Heavy on three of them. The company has not yet tried to catch Ship, which is a more difficult proposition, as the upper stage travels higher, farther and faster than the booster does.
Still, Musk is confident that SpaceX will pull off a Ship catch on the first try. (He did not give a specific target date for Flight 15, saying only that it was expected next month.)

"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," he said. "And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year, and and then accelerating next year."

Success would mean back-to-back Starship flights with huge milestones. On Flight 14, which occurred on Sept. 28, Ship reached orbit for the first time ever. It also deployed 26 of SpaceX's Starlink Version 3 satellites — the first 26 members of a next-gen broadband constellation in low Earth orbit that will eventually consist of about 100,000 spacecraft.

The Starship Flight 15 preview was something of an aside during today's call. The event primarily served to announce SpaceX's financial performance during Q3, the three-month stretch that ended on Sept. 30.

And that performance was strong, company representatives said. SpaceX recorded revenues of $14.6 billion during Q3, an increase of 161% from the $5.6 billion earned during Q3 of 2025. The company had a net income of $4.4 billion during Q3, $5.5 billion better than the result from the same stretch last year, when SpaceX lost $1.1 billion.

Just $1.8 billion of 2026 Q3 revenue came from SpaceX's launch division. The vast majority was generated by two other segments — connectivity (services provided by its Starlink megaconstellation) and artificial intelligence (or, as the Trump administration has recently rebranded it, "superintelligence").

SpaceX thinks these latter two segments will continue to boom. That's why it's building the infrastructure to support thousands of Starship launches per year — to loft lots of Starlink satellites and AI data centers to Earth orbit. And the company believes that it's positioned to really start raking in the cash, starting as soon as next year.
"In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of '27 is somewhere between 500 billion [dollars] and a trillion," Musk said.

On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. This was the last mission in the Zond program.

After the first three Zond missions explored Venus and Mars, the next ones were circumlunar missions that flew around the moon before returning to Earth. Although there was no crew on board, the Zond spacecraft was designed with cosmonauts in mind.

The Zond missions served as test flights for the Soviet Union's plans to send cosmonauts to the moon. But those plans for crewed flights never came to fruition. This was partly because the U.S. had already put astronauts on the moon, but also because the Zond missions had a lot of technical problems.

Zond 8 was considered a success — even though its guidance system malfunctioned on the way back to Earth. The spacecraft still returned to Earth safely and splashed down in the Indian Ocean one week after it launched.

While the Zond 1 and Zond 2 missions were launched toward Venus and Mars, respectively, the primary target of most Zond missions was the moon. At the time, the Soviet Union was embroiled in an ongoing space race with the United States to be the first on the moon with a human crew.

By the time Zond 8 launched on Oct. 20, 1970, that space race was lost to the Soviet Union. NASA and the U.S. had already landed astronauts on the moon twice with Apollo 11 and Apollo 12 (in July and November of 1969, respectively), and even peformed the first space rescue fo the Apollo 13 astronauts in April 1970.

While Zond 8 was uncrewed, it was a test flight of the Soviet Union's L1 spacecraft that was designed to fly a cosmonaut around the moon. It looped around the moon in a lunar flyby, approaching within 1,120 kilometers of the moon's surface at its closest point, according to RussianSpaceWeb.com.
Cameras on Zond 8 captured stunning views of the Earth and moon, recreating the iconic Earthrise views seen by Apollo 8 astronauts two years earlier in 1968.

Zond 8 ultimately splashed down in the Indian Ocean on Oct. 27, 1970 after a solar attitude sensor failed, sending it on a shorter, steeper reentry path during landing, according to RussianSpaceWeb.com. It was retrieved by a recovery ship, marking the end of the Soviet moon landing program. Russian would go on to develop a series of Salyut space stations, culminating in the long-lived Mir space station.

After decades without a moon probe, Russia did launch a new uncrewed moon lander in 2023. That Luna 25 mission failed and crashed into the lunar surface after an onboard engine controller malfunctioned. The country has pledged a return to the moon in 2027.

Taschen, purveyors of fine art and design special-edition books, have teamed up with George Lucas and his newly opened Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles to present a masterful two-volume catalog of the museum’s illuminating offerings.

Housed in a sturdy slipcase, readers will discover a pair of lavishly illustrated volumes spanning 832 pages and tipping the scales at nearly 14 pounds. At $200 for the pair, it's not cheap, but look on the bright side; hoisting these illustrated tomes will save you a subscription to your local gym!

This immersive collection documents in great detail the astounding scope of rare items on display in Lucas’s treasury of paintings, murals, photographs, sculptures, posters, comic strips, illustrations, costumes, and magazine covers that have spurred humankind’s imagination.
Developed in collaboration with George Lucas and the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, this extensive two-volume catalog brings together an unparalleled collection of narrative art.
We'd absolutely recommend checking out the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in person if you can.

Our own Chelsea Gohd visited the Los Angeles-based museum ahead of its opening in September 2026 and adored it. But if you're not a California local, getting lost in this collection's glossy pages is the next best thing to roaming the museum exhibitions on a rainy afternoon.

Far beyond a mere companion to the marvels inside the fantastic spaceship-shaped building poised near the University of Southern California campus — the same institution where Lucas attended film school in the late 1960s — these bold editions are an adventure in their own right.

Waiting to be absorbed is an impressive assortment of storytelling expression that showcases beautiful works by everyone from Maxfield Parrish, N.C. Wyeth, and Norman Rockwell to Frank Frazetta, Jack Kirby, and Ralph McQuarrie. Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, curated the museum’s contents that represent decades of collecting narrative art in all of its forms.

Our friends at Taschen were gracious enough to send us one of these Lucas Museum of Narrative Art special editions, and in unboxing this magnificent pair of books, one can feel the quality in the deluxe binding and thick covers. Inside you’ll find an eye-popping array of full-color photography and sharp descriptions for hundreds of artworks, all hand-picked by Lucas and Hobson.

Lucas himself delivers the preface, which is titled "The Art of Story," where he professes his love of art, myth, anthropology, illustrators, and cinema. He recalls when he came to meet his mentor, Professor Joseph Campbell, and how he amassed 40,000 pieces of art beginning when he was a student at USC.
The great director Guillermo del Toro provides a heartfelt foreword praising the importance of the museum and these prestigious companion volumes depicting a multitude of visual wonders.

Between the duo of volumes, sections are divided into chapters dealing with topics such as history, children's stories, the American West, everyday life, romance and adventure, photography, science fiction and fantasy, and, of course, Star Wars in Motion.

They take you on an overwhelming journey through the gallery’s incredibly diverse holdings, not least of which are archival items and concept art chronicling Lucas's involvement in the galaxy far, far away.

This remarkable "Star Wars" section will be of particular interest to sci-fi aficionados, as it contains 100 pages of original props, paintings, concept artwork, costumes, models, and digital renderings created by some of Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic’s best and brightest talents.

Taken with the rest of the 832 combined pages of Taschen's ambitious release that fully captures the dizzying breadth of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, it's a brilliant keepsake to spark your soul and imagination.

Scientists discover a way to kill dangerous gut bacteria without killing the good
- Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research

- Scientists have discovered a natural compound that targets dangerous C. difficile bacteria without wiping out the gut's beneficial microbes. Successful early tests suggest it could lead to a gentler, more effective treatment for stubborn intestinal infections that frequently return.

A dangerous intestinal infection may soon have a more targeted treatment option. Scientists have identified a natural compound that can kill the bacteria responsible for severe gut infections while leaving much of the beneficial gut microbiome unharmed.

The bacterium Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) is naturally found in the intestines of many people and generally causes no problems when present in small amounts. However, antibiotics that target a wide range of bacteria can upset the delicate balance of microorganisms in the gut. This disruption allows C. difficile to multiply rapidly, potentially causing severe intestinal inflammation that can become chronic.

C. difficile infections (CDI) are among the leading causes of diarrhea associated with antibiotic treatment. The bacteria produce toxins that can trigger dangerous and sometimes life-threatening inflammation in the intestines. Because these infections frequently return after treatment, scientists are searching for more effective ways to eliminate the pathogen without causing additional damage to the gut microbiome.

A team led by Prof. Rolf Müller, department head and scientific director at HIPS, has now identified a promising drug candidate that specifically targets C. difficile while preserving much of the gut's beneficial microbial community. HIPS is a site of the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI) that operates in collaboration with Saarland University.
Natural Compound Targets Dangerous Gut Bacteria

The researchers found that argyrin B, a naturally occurring antibacterial substance, was highly effective against C. difficile in laboratory tests and experiments involving infected mice. Importantly, the compound showed little activity against the beneficial microorganisms that help maintain a healthy digestive system.

"We were able to show that the natural compound argyrin B is highly effective against CDI: both in laboratory experiments and in a mouse model of the infection, where it significantly reduces the bacterial load," says Dr. Jennifer Herrmann, senior scientist in the department "Microbial Natural Products" at HIPS. "An antibacterial target of the argyrins had previously been identified and characterized in the notorious hospital-acquired pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Now we have been able to show that argyrin B also acts on this target in C. difficile and exhibits particularly high efficacy in doing so. In contrast, the argyrins have virtually no effect on the beneficial microorganisms in our digestive tract. The gut microbiome could therefore be spared during treatment with argyrin and restored to a healthy state more quickly."
A Bacteria-Killing Substance Found in Soil
Argyrins were originally discovered in myxobacteria, microorganisms that inhabit soil. These bacteria produce natural substances that help them attack other microbes and use them as a source of food.

Although argyrin B has demonstrated promising antibacterial activity, researchers must also determine whether its pharmaceutical properties make it suitable for use as a medicine. That includes understanding how the compound behaves inside the body and whether it could cause unwanted effects.

One particularly encouraging finding emerged when the team examined what happens after mice receive argyrin B orally. Very little of the compound entered their bloodstream. Instead, most of it remained in the large intestine, where C. difficile infections occur.

By concentrating in the gut rather than circulating throughout the body, argyrin B could potentially reduce the risk of side effects affecting other organs. Together with its selective activity against C. difficile, this characteristic makes the compound a promising candidate for a treatment that may be better tolerated.
Could It Help Prevent Recurring Gut Infections?

One of the biggest challenges in treating C. difficile is its tendency to return. Patients who experience multiple relapses are often treated using fecal microbiota transfer (commonly known as a stool transplant). This procedure aims to restore a healthier balance of gut microorganisms, but it can be complicated to perform and unpleasant for patients.

A medication developed from argyrin could eventually provide another treatment option. By eliminating the harmful bacteria without extensively disrupting the rest of the microbiome, such a therapy might reduce the likelihood of further infections and relapses. That could also help some patients avoid the need for stool transplants.

More research is needed before argyrin B can be considered for clinical use. The scientists plan to investigate which dosage produces the strongest antibacterial effect and use additional experimental models to determine whether the compound can also combat recurring C. difficile infections.

Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable

- The aging brain may be undergoing a remarkable transformation rather than simply losing its abilities, shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture. Scientists suggest this change could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.

Growing older is often associated with memory loss and declining mental abilities. However, scientists are questioning whether these changes tell the whole story. Rather than simply becoming less capable, the brain may be adapting to a new stage of life in which accumulated knowledge, wisdom, and understanding become more important than remembering every detail.

Researchers at the University of Arizona have proposed a different way of understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on findings from molecular biology and brain imaging, they suggest that the changes occurring in older brains may reflect a natural stage of human development rather than deterioration alone. Their work, published in Perspectives on Psychological Science, offers a new perspective on why thinking and memory change with age.

The researchers call their proposed explanation the adaptive aging hypothesis. It suggests that the brain gradually adjusts its priorities to make better use of a lifetime of accumulated experience. This could help explain why older adults often have valuable strengths in teaching, mentoring, storytelling, and passing knowledge to younger generations.

"If we look at normative aging as a story of just decline, we are really missing the boat," said study coauthor Fabian-Xosé Fernandez, an associate professor of cognition and neural systems at the University of Arizona. "The older brain is optimized for different things than the younger brain, predominantly the sharing of stored expertise and social relationships."
How the Brain Shifts From Memory to Meaning

Two brain regions play important roles in how people remember and interpret their experiences. The hippocampus helps preserve specific information about events, including their details and circumstances. The frontal cortex, meanwhile, is more involved in extracting broader meaning, recognizing patterns, and understanding the central message of an experience, sometimes called its "gist."

According to the researchers, the balance between these systems changes during healthy aging. As people grow older, the brain tends to place less emphasis on activity in the hippocampus and rely more on the frontal cortex. This shift may allow the brain to focus more on interpreting information through existing knowledge rather than recording every new experience in precise detail.

"The fact that you see this across people and animal models suggests there is an evolutionary driving force," Fernandez said. "One could argue you are developing your entire life, and development occurs in lockstep with the needs of your brain. When you're younger, the hippocampus turns on because you don't have a knowledge base or know how the world works. A kid absorbs information like a sponge because they are building an archive of information. In early life, the balance is tilted toward recollecting declarative memories with precision, detail, and context."

Young brains need to gather enormous amounts of new information because they are still building a foundation for understanding the world. By later adulthood, however, people have already developed extensive stores of memories, concepts, and experiences. Connecting new information to what they already know may become more useful than retaining every individual detail.

The researchers suggest that this changing balance reflects a shift in how the brain processes experience. Instead of concentrating primarily on collecting detailed memories, it increasingly emphasizes understanding relationships, identifying underlying meaning, and applying previously acquired knowledge.
Why Evolution May Favor Wisdom in Older Adults

Evidence of similar changes in animal models raises the possibility that this transition has an evolutionary explanation. Fernandez suggests that the aging brain may be adapting to help individuals preserve and share the knowledge they have acquired throughout their lives.

From this perspective, the ability to draw on decades of experience could be especially valuable for making judgments, guiding others, and transferring important information between generations. Older adults may therefore play a distinct role in supporting younger people through mentorship, teaching, and storytelling.

"Given those goals, it makes sense that you aren't interested in nitty-gritty details," Fernandez said. "You are interested in safeguarding the vast knowledge you already have. Evolution may be saying that if you make it long enough, there's a need to transmit this information, so we put into motion biological changes that enforce and protect your semantic and autobiographical memories."

Under this hypothesis, changes in memory and thinking are not necessarily signs that the brain is functioning less effectively. They may instead reflect a different set of priorities, with greater emphasis on preserving meaningful knowledge and using it to understand new situations.
Why Healthy Brain Aging Is Different From Alzheimer's
The adaptive aging hypothesis could also provide scientists with another way to examine the differences between normal cognitive aging and Alzheimer's disease.

Although both involve changes in memory, Fernandez emphasizes that Alzheimer's should not be understood as ordinary aging taken to an extreme. The biological processes involved are fundamentally different.
"When I was in grad school, people thought about Alzheimer's as a more intense version of cognitive aging, but that is just not the case," Fernandez said. "They are completely different."

During typical aging, the brain's gradual shift away from relying heavily on the hippocampus and toward greater involvement of the frontal cortex generally unfolds between the fifth and seventh decades of life. In Alzheimer's disease, however, abnormal processes involving proteins such as amyloid and tau may interfere with this transition.

One important distinction involves activity in the hippocampus. While healthy aging is generally associated with reduced emphasis on this region, Alzheimer's can involve unusually high levels of hippocampal activity. Rather than supporting the normal progression of cognitive development, disease-related changes may disrupt the brain networks responsible for memory and understanding.

"In normative aging, hippocampal activation is deemphasized, which is probably what should be happening in a 70-year-old. But in many cases of Alzheimer's, it turns out the hippocampus is hyperactive," he said. "This beautiful developmental transition is completely disrupted in Alzheimer's disease by pathological processes that mess with episodic memory and interfere with circuits that allow you to think about your own life, lexicon, and vocabulary."

These disruptions can affect the ability to recall personal experiences and access stored knowledge, including words and their meanings. Understanding how these changes differ from the adaptations associated with healthy aging may help researchers develop a clearer picture of normal brain development and neurodegenerative disease.
Embracing the Hidden Strengths of the Aging Brain

The researchers argue that society may need to reconsider what successful brain aging looks like. Encouraging older adults to process information exactly as younger people do may not always be the most productive approach.

Fernandez suggests that placing excessive emphasis on remembering precise details could work against the brain's changing priorities. "For many individuals, the weight of how you process information should probably not be so hippocampal-centric by the sixth or seventh decade."

Instead of judging older adults primarily by abilities that tend to weaken with age, the researchers encourage greater recognition of the capabilities that may become especially valuable later in life.

Creating more opportunities for social interaction could be one way to support these strengths. Relationships between older and younger generations may be particularly beneficial because they provide opportunities to exchange experiences, share expertise, and preserve knowledge that might otherwise be lost.

"People see older individuals and look at them as not being on par with younger individuals across a lot of metrics," Fernandez says. "The way I look at it is that you've got someone with a brain that has been active for several decades and has seen a lot. There is tremendous value there, and we don't do a good job of unlocking it."

The central message of the adaptive aging hypothesis is that growing older may involve more than a gradual reduction in cognitive abilities. Although some mental skills become less reliable with age, the brain may also be adapting to make better use of the knowledge and experience accumulated over a lifetime. Recognizing those strengths could change how society understands aging and the contributions older adults can make.

To us mortals, the flow of time goes one way.
Yesterday is gone, tomorrow is yet to come, and no matter how precisely and faithfully a clock marks the passing seconds, we can never return to a moment that has passed.
But for a time crystal, things are very different.

The constituent ranks of this mysterious state of matter – be they atoms, sound waves, or topological defects – are strictly regimented in time, a repeating pattern of beats that could be snipped from a recording at regular intervals and perfectly superimposed, one over another.
Once thought impossible, time crystals have been observed in systems from physical atomic lattices to levitating styrofoam.

Now, physicists have discovered a strange new way for a time crystal to emerge – not through the imposition of an external rhythm, but through a spontaneous process in which competing vibrations gradually fall into step – order gradually emerging from chaos.

Using a 3D-printed two-dimensional metamaterial, an international team of physicists led by Jonas Veenstra of the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands observed small, rapid vibrations giving way to progressively larger, slower waves, until the entire structure was moving in synchrony.
The researchers call this process "wave coarsening", and it could reveal a new way for matter to organize itself into persistent patterns in time.
One of the biggest challenges to time crystal research is how devastatingly fragile these systems can be.

When you're trying to keep something in very precise step, even a slight disturbance can send it tumbling into disorder. In systems with only one or two spatial dimensions, those disturbances can be particularly destructive.
This makes the emergence of a stable, synchronized rhythm in a two-dimensional material especially intriguing.
One possible route to such order lies in the way different parts of a material interact with each other.
Veenstra and his colleagues wanted to observe what happens to waves in a system when the influence of one part of the system on another isn't necessarily reciprocated.

These are known as non-reciprocal interactions, and they can produce some peculiar dynamics. Under the right conditions, rather than settling into a jumble of competing oscillations, waves can gradually reorganize, with longer, slower patterns taking over from shorter, faster ones.
Eventually, a single coherent rhythm can emerge across the entire system.
To show that this can happen mathematically is one thing – but manifesting it in a real material is a bit trickier.
For this, the researchers built an unusual metamaterial – one whose properties emerge from its structure, rather than its composition.
It consisted of 37 units arranged in a honeycomb-like lattice, each made from three elastic hexagons fitted with sensors, actuators, and a tiny electronic controller.

The components were programmed to respond to one another in a very particular way. When one hexagon was compressed, its clockwise neighbor compressed too, while its counterclockwise neighbor expanded.
This asymmetrical response allowed the researchers to engineer the non-reciprocal interactions they wanted to study.
They gave the honeycomb a nudge, introducing small, random disturbances into the structure, and watched what happened.

At first, the individual units began vibrating rapidly, at around 30 times per second. But gradually, larger waves emerged, traveling around the material's edge, overwhelming the smaller oscillations.
Then, as the waves grew longer, their oscillations slowed until the entire honeycomb was moving together in a single, synchronized rhythm.
Anyone can make a wave, though. The next part is demonstrating that the wave is a time crystal.
For that, the researchers needed to establish that the synchronized oscillations weren't just a fleeting phenomenon, but a form of order that could persist even when jostled by random disturbances.
They turned to mathematical analysis and computer simulations, introducing noise into their model to see whether it would destroy the synchronized rhythm.
It didn't. Their results showed that the oscillations could remain coherent despite the disturbances, even as the system approached an effectively infinite size.

The honeycomb wasn't the end of the experiments, either. The researchers wanted to know if the effect could emerge in a system with a different architecture – so they built a donut for waves to ride, like an extraordinarily weird mechanical bull crossed with air hockey.

It consisted of a single elastic ring fitted with 24 motors, programmed to produce non-reciprocal interactions between neighboring sections. They placed it on an air table, allowing it to float with minimal friction.
When they activated the motors and disturbed the ring, waves began to travel around its circumference, deforming it into a succession of shifting polygonal shapes.
As the waves grew longer and slower, the polygons developed fewer sides, until the ring's motion was dominated by a single large-scale pattern.
The researchers did not separately establish that this system also formed a time crystal, but it did reveal something important about wave coarsening.

Their mathematical analysis showed that, as the waves grow in amplitude, they change the dynamics of the system, increasingly favoring waves with longer wavelengths. Those larger waves then grow stronger, further shifting the balance in their favor.
This creates a feedback loop in which the dominant waves become progressively larger and slower, until they reach the limits imposed by the size of the material itself.
Rather than having to impose a synchronized rhythm from outside, the researchers found a way for the material to organize its own vibrations.
Finally, there was one more surprise. The researchers also found that the process could be interrupted.

In their mathematical model, adding friction changed which waves were able to grow. The longest waves were suppressed, preventing the vibrations from continuing to reorganize into ever-larger patterns.
Instead of the entire material falling into step, the system could settle into a different kind of order – persistent waves traveling in one direction along its edge.

This suggests that the same underlying physics could produce different kinds of organized motion, depending on the conditions. By understanding how to control those conditions, researchers may eventually find new ways to guide vibrations through engineered materials.
The discovery could have implications for fields ranging from acoustics to soft robotics, although practical applications remain some way off.

But perhaps the most exciting part is that the researchers didn't need to induce and guide the rhythm of the material's vibrations. By engineering how its components interacted, they created conditions in which the vibrations could organize themselves.
Their results suggest that this self-organization could offer a new route to the robust, long-lasting temporal order that has proved so difficult to achieve in time crystals.

"We anticipate that wave coarsening represents an exemplary route towards time-crystallization in systems with additional symmetries and associated Goldstone modes," they write, "which can be leveraged as a control strategy for shape changes and directed motion in fields such as robotics, active matter and optomechanics with non-reciprocal phase transitions."
The research has been published in Nature.
Many people with depression don't respond to existing treatments, and scientists think it might be because of the many different routes people can take to arrive at the same depressive symptoms.
A new study found a quarter of patients fit into a 'circadian' subtype of depression, arising from a state of perpetual jet lag.
Led by psychiatry researchers Jacob Crouse and Ian Hickie, a team from the University of Sydney in Australia has published its findings in the British Journal of Psychiatry.

Current clinical guidelines treat depression as one disorder. But Hickie and team believe that while depression may look similar for each patient, many different biological problems may be driving the symptoms.
Most available treatments for depression assume the disorder is underpinned by anxiety. But for the 30 percent of young people with atypical depression, that is not the case.
So, Hickie asks, if it's not underpinned by anxiety, then what is driving it?
"What we've been investigating for some time now is the neurobiology of the brain regulators of the circadian system," he says.
The circadian systems in our body are those that are aligned with the 24-hour day and night cycle, with light being the main signal modulating these systems. But every body is a little bit different.
"The co-ordination of those clocks underpins your mood, your metabolism, your concentration, your sleep/wake cycle, and many other key factors," Hickie explains.
"When it's off, you feel jet-lagged all the time. You feel tired, you feel exhausted, you gain weight, you can't concentrate, you sleep poorly, and your behavior changes."

Hickie and his colleagues have now found evidence that this basic mechanism does indeed underlie a proportion of mood disorders, in data from 11,380 participants in the ongoing Australian Genetics of Depression Study.
The researchers define the circadian subtype of depression with six criteria.

For someone with circadian depression, their symptoms will change with the seasons, due to the shifting day lengths. Secondly, the midpoint of their sleep is delayed compared to the general population.

They also experience social jet lag: that is, their sleep midpoint on working days is several hours different than the midpoint on non-working days (i.e., their sleep tendencies do not match the timing that society is typically designed around).

They have an evening chronotype, and when given the opportunity, they will sleep longer than the typical person (perhaps, the researchers suggest, because of the constant experience of jet lag). Unsurprisingly, they also report being very tired in the morning.
Among the 11,380 people included in this study, about 1 in 4 patients fit into this circadian subtype.

There was some overlap with other proposed depression subtypes. The greatest crossover was with atypical depression, but even then, about 1,400 cases met the criteria for atypical depression but not the circadian subtype, which suggests these may still be distinct forms of the disorder.

"Depression is not a uniform illness and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes mean that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them," explains Emiliana Tonini, first author on the new paper.
Participants with the circadian subtype started experiencing depression earlier in life and reported more severe clinical features like mania, psychosis, and suicidality.

They were also more likely to experience weight gain during depressive episodes. They also had a higher genetic risk for major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD, and inflammatory and cardiovascular health problems.
These participants were also less likely to find common antidepressant medications effective, and tended to experience more side effects from the medications.

"Because circadian depression is linked to people's internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation," Crouse says.
"For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances."

On the long drive to my kid’s sporting event this weekend, most drivers, myself included, cruised a few miles over the speed limit. A few drivers, though, blazed past in the left lane. Mindful of safety — and police cruisers — I didn’t follow suit.

Left unchecked though, a few bad actors can trigger social breakdown, researchers report October 21 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The truly deviant among us “basically take off the guardrails of the group,” says Lucas Molleman, a psychologist at the University of Amsterdam.

Molleman and his colleagues designed a thought experiment to show what it takes to sway people to bend or break the rules. They picked a contentious time: A week before the 2024 U.S. presidential election. The team recruited 750 U.S. participants, with roughly half identifying as Democrats and half as Republicans. The online participants watched an animated shooting star streak across a row of 100 squares and then selected which square shone the brightest.

Though the brightest square always appeared around the row’s middle, participants received more money for selecting squares farther to the right (the farthest-right square netted participants roughly the equivalent of $1.30). Dedicated rule followers, or those who always followed the rules, and rule breakers, existed in roughly equal numbers, with each comprising about a fifth of the larger group, initial tests showed.

The researchers then stirred the pot. Participants repeated the simple experiment several times while receiving information about a previous respondent, including their political affiliation and level of adherence to the rule. Rule followers rarely begot more rule followers, even when respondents belonged to the same political party, the team found.

The reverse held true for rule breakers, though. Receiving information that someone with the same political leanings had just disregarded the rules shifted selections rightward on average. Absent social cues, participants selected the farthest-right square roughly 23 percent of the time. That increased to almost 40 percent of the time after participants learned that a political comrade had made the most lucrative choice. Bad behavior, in other words, was contagious.
Most individuals’ rule-breaking levels mirrored or stayed below that of others. But just over 4 percent of individuals escalated deviant behavior beyond that of the previous respondent.

The researchers then created a computer simulation to see how those rule-breaking behaviors might play out across time. They designed a digital twin for each of the 750 participants and had the doppelgängers interact in groups of 100. In some scenarios, those few escalation-prone individuals could push everyone in the group toward wild rule breaking. But if the 100-twin selection had the same proportion of dedicated rule followers as the human experiment, overall deviance settled at a more intermediate level.

This study provides some keen insights into how humans might behave absent consequences, says behavioral economist Eugen Dimant of the University of Pennsylvania. “But that’s not how the world works.” His work suggests that to truly understand social contagion and the emergence of mobs, researchers must consider societal forces, such as punishments and social norms, that tend to keep behavior in check.

To Molleman, though, the study’s insights into individual behaviors are key. This pared-down experiment shows how just a few bad actors can cause entire groups to spiral out of control. Such findings could underpin everything from collective speeding to peaceful protests that turn violent, he says. “This is fundamental science … Obviously reality is way more complex.”

Actress Christina Applegate’s announcement on Tuesday that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) in 2021 immediately made headlines. Her experience, while not the norm, is far from unusual, experts say.

Applegate disclosed the revelation on an episode of her podcast with Jamie Lynn Sigler, MeSsy, which centers on their lives with MS. (Sigler disclosed that she has relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, or RRMS, in 2016.) “In January of 2021, I had numbness in my toes, and that numbness grew to all of my legs,” Applegate recalled on the podcast. “And then the pain started.”
After rounds of tests for a variety of conditions, her doctor found “almost 40” lesions on her brain and diagnosed her with MS, she said.
