MS can be devastating. The neurological condition causes the body’s immune system to attack the nervous system, including parts of the brain. Symptoms can include fatigue, mood changes, dizziness, vision issues and numbness in the arms and legs.
Now, five years later, Applegate said that, after analyzing brain scans with a “new technology,” her doctor told her she doesn’t have MS. “I’m back at square one,” she said.
Her experience is more common than you might think.

“Diagnosing MS is a little bit like putting a puzzle together,” says Bruce Bebo, chief research and medical affairs officer at the National Multiple Sclerosis Society. “There’s not a single diagnostic test that tells you, ‘You have MS.’” The disease’s symptoms overlap with other conditions, such as neuromyelitis optica, which have to be ruled out before a diagnosis can be made.

Estimates vary, but a recent meta-analysis found that around 15 percent of MS cases across studies were misdiagnoses. The absolute odds of a misdiagnosis can vary by patient population and clinical setting, however, Bebo says. For instance, a study performed at a patient referral center where MS patients have been sent for additional analysis may inherently show higher rates of misdiagnosis in that patient population, says Thomas Flagiello, a neurologist at NYU Langone.
Overall, “although misdiagnosis happens, the majority of cases are correctly diagnosed,” Flagiello says.

Diagnostic tools are getting better. In 2025 the International Advisory Committee on Clinical Trials in Multiple Sclerosis updated its guidelines on how to diagnose MS to reflect recent advancements, including the ability to look in brain scans for specific clues, such as the central vein sign, a small vein running through brain lesions, or a specific kind of brain feature called a paramagnetic rim lesion, Bebo says.
Identifying these markers in patients’ brains could help reduce misdiagnoses, Bebo says. But as of now, it’s impossible to totally rule out a misdiagnosis.
As Applegate’s story illustrates, the consequences of a misdiagnosis can be substantial. It could mean someone receives treatment they don’t need—or misses out on treatment that they do, Bebo says.

That’s why getting a diagnosis right “really matters,” Bebo says. “Whether you have MS or you ultimately have some other condition, people experiencing significant neurologic symptoms deserve to have a careful evaluation.”

On September 4, 2026, the United Nations adopted a resolution to promote a new map of the world. The resolution encourages governments, schools and organizations to replace the much-criticized Mercator projection, which significantly overestimates the size of countries and continents near the poles, with the area-preserving Equal Earth projection developed in 2018.

The move sparked a lot of chatter. Some called the decision a step to dismantle “cartographic colonialism,” others a “radical ideological project.” In total, 164 nations voted in favor of the proposal, six abstained, and the U.S. was the only country to vote against. The resolution is not legally binding, but it sends a clear signal to use a fairer (and more accurate) representation of our world in the future.

Creating a suitable map of Earth might not sound too difficult at first. But mathematics makes it an unsolvable problem: a sphere cannot be mapped onto a flat plane. Try to wrap a spherical object in gift paper, for instance, and you will inevitably crease the paper. Cartographers have been aware of this challenge for centuries. It is impossible to design a world map that accurately depicts both the precise shape of the continents and countries and their area simultaneously. Compromises—and heated debates—are unavoidable.

In 1569 scholar Gerardus Mercator developed a projection, now named after him, that accurately depicts angles on a sphere. With this approach, all continents and countries retain their shape, which is particularly advantageous for seafarers. Using a Mercator projection, a compass course corresponds to a straight line on the map. For centuries, this world map was the standard.

To obtain the Mercator projection, a cylindrical map is placed around Earth so that it touches the globe along the equator. Then every point on Earth is projected onto the cylinder from Earth’s center. The result is that countries near the poles are enlarged such that Greenland (836,330 square miles) and Africa (11.7 million square miles) appear roughly the same size on this map—even though Africa is 14 times as large.

In the 20th century, German historian Arno Peters objected to the Eurocentric worldview and the ways this map contributed to it. He called for a new representation and, in 1973, designed an equal-area projection. Technically cartographer James Gall developed a similar world map a century earlier, but it received little attention at the time.

To obtain this Gall–Peters projection, a cylindrical map is used, similar to the Mercator projection. In this case, however, the points of the globe are not projected onto the map from Earth’s center but along horizontal lines. The result is an equal-area representation: the sizes of the countries on the globe correspond to those on the map.

But critics raised several objections to this map, including the significant distortions to the shapes of countries and continents. Countries in low latitudes become especially warped in this presentation.

In March 2017 the Boston public school system announced its intention to replace its Mercator projection maps with the Gall-Peters projection. In response, software developer Bojan Šavrič of the Californian company Esri and cartographers Tom Patterson of the U.S. National Park Service and Bernhard Jenny of Monash University in Australia began searching for more suitable equal-area projections. And when they could not find an option that met all of their aesthetic criteria, they decided to develop something new that they called Equal Earth.

The researchers based their work on the Robinson projection, developed in the early 1960s. This is a variant of the world map that is neither area-preserving nor angle-preserving. Unlike the previously mentioned examples, it does not correspond to a mathematical projection, meaning it has no underlying formulas that generate it. Instead it is constructed using a table of empirically determined reference points. The points in between these reference points are determined by interpolation. While this may seem unscientific, the result appears natural: the Robinson map only shows significant deviations in angle and area in the polar regions.

Šavrič, Patterson and Jenny aimed to create a similarly natural effect but wanted to preserve the area of various landmasses. In 2018 they published their Equal Earth map in the International Journal of Geographical Information Science. It is a pseudocylindrical projection: Latitude lines are represented as straight lines, as in ordinary cylindrical projections, but longitude lines are not (except for the prime meridian).

They determined the details of the new world map in two steps: First, the researchers combined two existing projections using custom-developed graphics software. This visual approach allowed them to create a subjectively appealing appearance for the coordinate grid and the continental landmasses. The second step involved calculating the corresponding projection equations.

“Generally speaking, there are no truly ‘perfect’ maps,” cartographer Lorenz Hurni of the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich told Swiss broadcaster SRF. “This map seeks a compromise to minimize the distortion of the shapes of countries and continents.” That’s why many countries—including members of the African Union—consider it the best possible representation of a world map. The state of Togo therefore introduced the new resolution at the United Nations, entitled “Correct the Map,” on its behalf in an aim to establish the Equal Earth map as the standard.

Although the U.N. flag uses a completely different representation of the world (an equidistant azimuthal projection that has been artistically corrected along the lines of latitude), many hope that the U.N. resolution will gradually be implemented throughout the world, updating the way we look at it.

This problem is the result of many hours of cleaning baby bottles for two daughters. Suppose your baby uses a certain type of bottle that is composed of three pieces (say, top, middle and bottom). The bottles come in two colors (say, blue and green). You have three blue bottles and two green bottles, for a total of five bottles. Your baby uses all five bottles in a single day. Because you’re perpetually tired, you do not disassemble and wash the bottles until the end of the day. After the bottles have dried overnight, you reassemble them and begin your next day. Such is the life of a new parent.

When you go to reassemble the bottles, you notice that you can exchange parts among them so that some are “mixed up.” For example, you can put a green top on a blue middle and blue bottom. Naturally, you try your hand at swapping parts so there is no complete bottle of a single color—in other words, you find a “derangement” of the bottles.
Suppose you then buy some new bottles in a third color (say, pink). What is the minimum number of pink bottles required to ensure that no derangement can occur?

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will discuss refining Western energy supplies with Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries when he visits the company's plant in Jamnagar, Gujarat — the world's largest single-site refinery.

The U.S. is looking to "work together more closely" with Reliance for refining energy from the "Western Hemisphere," Rubio said in an interview with India's Network 18, which is owned by Reliance. "I think that's helpful to India, but it's also helpful to us," he added.

Reliance's Jamnagar refinery, which Rubio will visit on Wednesday, has a crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day. Reliance has also emerged as the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude outside of the U.S., as of end-September.
The company's "extraordinary" refining capacity could help India diversify its energy supplies, Rubio said, hinting at possibly greater offtake of Venezuelan crude.

"We think there's an opportunity for them [Reliance Industries] to continue to help India diversify its supply chain, its supply of energy," Rubio said, adding that Venezuela was ramping up energy production, and that "India has had a long history of being able to refine some of that."

U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing India to buy more Venezuelan oil to replace Russian barrels, and while state-owned oil companies are making opportunistic purchases, Reliance has been the primary buyer.

Beyond oil purchases, Reliance has been deepening ties with the U.S. this year, with Trump announcing in March that America will build its first new oil refinery in 50 years, helped by investment from Ambani's Reliance.
While Reliance has not confirmed the size of investment, Trump in a Truth Social post had said that "THIS IS A HISTORIC $300 BILLION DOLLAR DEAL — THE BIGGEST IN U.S. HISTORY."

Reliance has never made an announcement about the refinery investment, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC, adding that it creates an air of uncertainty around the deal. Rubio would seek to "clinch" that deal or take it a little further, Chaudhuri said.
Rubio told Network 18 that Reliance had "invested in increasing the refining capacity within the United States."

His visit to Jamnagar also comes at a time when diesel prices have surged in the U.S., with midterm elections looming. Diesel prices, which affect American truckers, farmers, and shippers, are expected to remain elevated going into next year.

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Rubio underscored Reliance's ability to refine heavy crude and referred to India as a "refining superpower" when asked about the role New Delhi and its companies can play in meeting the world's energy demand.
Indian and Chinese refineries are good at handling heavy and medium-heavy crude from Venezuela and Russia, Chaudhuri said, adding that this grade of fuel is better-suited for producing diesel.

Shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast, citing power supply delays at its Melbourne facility amid local community and stakeholder opposition.

The company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to between $475 million Australian dollars and A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million forecast earlier, while cutting its underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million from A$385 million to A$410 million.

The delays to power stem from the suspension of infrastructure upgrades at the company's M3 Melbourne data center amid community opposition, with electricity distributor Jemena not expecting to resume work before February 2027, according to NextDC.
Jemena cited safety concerns and restricted access to work sites due to community opposition, as well as a lack of consent from the local council pending further community consultation.
Citi said in a note that NextDC's power delays could affect earnings beyond fiscal 2027, citing delays to approvals for the M3 expansion and a longer-than-expected timeline for transformer upgrades.

As Australia grapples with growing concerns over the impact of data center developments on local communities, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government was working to establish national standards for investment.

Chalmers told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Wednesday that the government welcomes investment in data centers and AI infrastructure, provided it aligns with the country's national interest, adding that the government was finalizing national investment standards to address concerns surrounding AI deployment.

Australia is not alone in facing opposition to data center projects, there has been growing push back against data center developments worldwide, amid concerns over their impact on local communities and the environment.
NextDC shares have declined for seven straight weeks, and are on course to end lower for the eighth week.
James Bond fans are likely to be shaken by an auction set to honor the beloved franchise.

Propstore’s online Bond auction features 400 lots spanning every film in the long-running series and highlighting the franchise’s evolution, from 1962’s Dr. No through 2021’s No Time to Die. The James Bond Online Auction is now available for worldwide bids, which can be placed through the auction link, and it runs until Oct. 27.

The auction’s highlights include Daniel Craig‘s Tom Ford suit, shirt and cufflinks from 2012’s Skyfall, expected to sell for as much as $53,000. Also hitting the block are Ana de Armas‘ Paloma dress and sandals from No Time to Die, with the outfit likely to go for around $53,000.

One lucky bidder will end up with a set of 14 first-edition books by Bond author Ian Fleming, with the collection from publishing firm Jonathan Cape expected to sell for upwards of $50,000. A linen-backed British quad poster for Dr. No is valued at as much as $22,000, while a clapperboard from 1983’s Octopussy could be headed for a sale above $10,000.

“James Bond has a unique place in popular culture, and interest remains strong to this day,” Propstore director of consignments Alastair McCrea tells The Hollywood Reporter. “Bond has been part of cinema for over 60 years, with each generation having its own Bond, its own favorite film and memorable moments. One person grew up with Sean Connery, another with Pierce Brosnan, another with Daniel Craig, so you can still have three generations of the same family debating over who the best 007 is. That’s what makes collecting Bond so appealing; there’s something for everyone, whether it’s the films, the actors, the gadgets, posters, costumes or the original artwork. Very few film franchises can claim that, and it’s a big part of why the collecting market remains so strong.”

This follows Propstore’s previous online auction that featured more than 300 items from director Denis Villeneuve‘s Blade Runner 2049. That auction concluded last week, with such highlights as the signature coat worn by Ryan Gosling, which sold for $201,600, including the buyer’s premium. This Bond-focused sale takes place as anticipation builds amid the ongoing casting process for the star of the next 007 movie that Villeneuve is set to direct.

“The news about a new movie on the horizon always piques renewed interest, and I expect that to grow over the forthcoming years,” adds McCrea. “The links to other brands have also kept the interest high, from Aston Martin to Omega, and they all add to the exposure. The Daniel Craig era saw the biggest price rise in collectables, and this can be seen across the areas of posters, scripts, books and costumes.”
It was a night to remember on Dancing with the Stars, as the 10 Things I Hate About You cast reunited on the ABC dance competition show to pay tribute to the late Heath Ledger.

Ahead of Tuesday’s episode, which was Dedication Night, it was revealed that Julia Stiles and her pro partner Ezra Sosa would be dedicating their dance to Ledger, who starred opposite Stiles in the beloved 1999 rom-com.

The pair danced to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You” by Frankie Valli, which was the song Ledger’s Patrick Verona serenaded Stiles’ Kat Stratford with during her soccer practice at the high school stadium. In the scene, he runs and dances across the stands as the marching band plays to try and win her over after Joey Donner (Andrew Keegan) pays him to take Kat out.

Following Stiles and Sosa’s emotional dance, which featured some of Ledger’s iconic moves, the poem her character reads in the film about Patrick starts playing in the ballroom. After the actress lays a flower on the ground in honor of Ledger, she is joined by her fellow co-stars, including Keegan, Joseph Gordon-Levitt (Cameron James), Larisa Oleynik (Bianca Stratford), Gabrielle Union (Chastity) and Susan May Pratt (Mandella).
Ahead of the new DWTS episode, Sosa took to Instagram to share how important this dance was for both of them.

“I don’t think we’ve every approached a performance with more care, sensitivity, and intention than this one,” Sosa wrote in the joint post with Stiles. “From the very beginning it was incredibly important to both Julia and I that this tribute be created with the utmost respect, thoughtfulness, and close guidance from those who hold Heath and his memory closest. This isn’t about defining a relationship or telling a story that isn’t ours to tell. “We’ve poured so much love into this piece, and we’re incredibly grateful for the trust placed in us to bring it to life,” he added. “Our only hope is that it honors his memory with the dignity, love, and respect it deserves.”
Ledger died in 2008 at the age of 28 from an accidental overdose.

10 Things I Hate About You, directed by Gil Junger, follows teen Joey who wants to date Bianca, but she can’t date until her antisocial older sister, Kat, has a boyfriend, per her strict father’s rules. That’s when Joey pays a mysterious boy, Patrick, to ask Kat out.

Sacha Baron Cohen can go to the deepest well of characters, both comedic and dramatic. Think Ali G, Borat, Brüno, and… cellist.
On Tuesday night (Oct. 20), the British funnyman showed us another side, as he slipped into Beck’s strings ensemble for a performance on NBC’s The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon.

For a change, Cohen didn’t play for laughs. Or play anyone, for that matter. The Dictator actor flexed his musician muscles for a surprise back seat spot on the cello, supporting Beck on “In the Night.”

“In the Night” appears on Beck’s Ride Lonesome, a sweeping and delicate album that captures the sonic textures of his 2015 Grammy Award-winning album of the Year Morning Phase and its spiritual companion, Sea Change from 2002.

Ride Lonesome (via Capitol Records) dropped last month and is Beck’s first collection of all-new material since 2019’s Hyperspace. Watch his late night performance below, with a little help from Sasha Baron Cohen.

Earlier, Beck and Cohen sat for separate chats with Fallon. Beck spoke with the host on the inspiration behind his latest LP, the “austere” design of his tour in support of it, and recounted how Luke Wilson’s Hansel character in Zoolander was (maybe) based on him.
Beck confirmed that he was asked to be in Zoolander, but he “stupidly said no.” Instead, the producers got David Bowie.

Reflecting on Ride Lonesome, Beck reckons: “It’s a moody kinda stuff. It’s the mood of like when you’re in your house, it’s almost dark but you haven’t turned the lights on. It’s kinda like blue hour.”

Cohen, meanwhile, sat with Fallon for some insights into his mockumentary Ali G: Who Iz I?, for which he revives his breakthrough character Ali G. Cohen makes his feature directorial debut in Who Iz I?, which Amazon MGM Studios releases this Friday (Oct. 23) in cinemas for just one week, ahead of its streaming rollout on Prime Video.

A new Sasha Baron Cohen film is never without controversy. Who Iz I?, however, has been slammed by some activists as a racism hiding in plain sight. Cohen has responded with a cover essay for Time magazine, in which he writes, “The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him.” The world Ali G has “returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven’t just lingered—they’ve metastasized. They’re fueled by the greatest propaganda machine in history—social media—and now by its monstrous child, AI.”

SYDNEY, Australia — APRA AMCOS Group has posted all-time-high revenue of A$857.4 million ($599 million), up 8.8% from the previous financial year thanks to strong digital, international and public performance licensing.
At the same time, group net distributable revenue (NDR) ballooned to A$755.7 million ($528 million), up 10.6% year-on-year.

As APRA celebrates its 100th anniversary, the PRO’s international revenue lifts to a record-high of A$103.2 million ($72 million), powered by strong touring from the likes of Ninajirachi, and screen growth globally, led by animated kids show Bluey, reads a statement.

The engine room for APRA AMCOS is the “Digital” category, which represents more than 53% overall share, and up 12.5% from the same period last time, while OneMusic’s public performance revenue lifted 10.9% on strong gains from concerts and events, fitness and restaurants.

“Audiences continue to spend their entertainment dollars on large-scale, high-priced events like AC/DC, Ed Sheeran and Oasis,” reads a statement, “leading to softer sales and greater price sensitivity for mid-tier tours and smaller festivals.”
Published this week, it’s “another year of strong results for our members, with more money out the door to them than ever before,” explains Dean Ormston, CEO of APRA AMCOS.

Broken down, APRA generated A$557.2 million ($389 million) in revenue for the year, up 6.9%, while AMCOS posted A$300.2 million ($209 million), up 12.6%. Group expense-to-revenue ratio was 11.86%, down from 13.26%.

If there’s one clanger in APRA AMCOS’ 2026 Year In Review, for the period July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026, it’s raw proof that Australians and New Zealanders are tuning out of homegrown music. More than 91% of the music Australians streamed in FY26 was imported. It’s a worse situation across ditch, as 96% of music consumed in NZ was created by internationals.
“If the current trend continues, Australian members’ share of streaming is on track to fall to close to 5% within the next five years,” adds Ormston. “It’s a devastating statistic.”
APRA AMCOS serves more than 135,000 songwriter, composer and music publisher members. Despite the strong overall picture, Ormston assures the organization is focused on the challenges that lie ahead.

“We continue to work closely with governments, platforms and international partners to ensure members are askedpermission and receive payment when their works are used to train or generate AI content,” he explains.

In June, APRA AMCOS took that message to the CISAC General Assembly in Paris, where the Australasian body and its international partners set out the Paris Commitment to protect, recognize and fairly remunerate human creators. Then, its leadership assembled in the nation’s capital, Canberra, to call on the Australian Government to hold firm on the Copyright Act, in the face of lobbying from big tech for a TDM. “ We will continue making that case, clearly and consistently, for as long as it takes.”

And as AI technology advances, he adds, “so too does the need to defend the simple principle at the heart of copyright: creators must retain the right to control the use of their work and be paid when that work is used. Our position remains clear and simple: permission and payment.”

It’s official: Powderfinger’s reunion tour is Australia’s hottest ticket.
Following Monday’s general public onsale, upwards of 300,000 tickets were snapped up for next years’ comeback run, reps say.
That means every seat across the rockers’ 26-date 2027 national tour is completely sold out, besting the onsale for Powderfinger’s 2010 Sunsets Farewell Tour.

“It’s a staggering show of love for a band whose songs have soundtracked so many lives, and a clear sign that this reunion tour means as much to the fans as it does to the band,” reads a statement from the band.
With that show of love, Powderfinger will lock in more shows in “select destinations that allows as many people as possible to get their hands on tickets.”

As previously reported, the beloved Australian rock band will embark on a rare jaunt next year, pre-sales for which opened last Wednesday, Oct. 14. The 18 coast-to-coast concerts that were initially announced for September and October 2027, quickly grew to 26 with dates extending into November.

“We know many of you missed out and we know how disappointing that is,” reads a statement from the band, issued following Monday’s general onsale. Please know we hear you, and we have your back. Right now, the team is locking in one final encore run of shows that will close out this tour and we’ll share the details as soon as they’re confirmed.”

In the meantime, the message continues, “we ask for just a little more patience. Please don’t lose heart. Bringing extra dates together takes time but we’re working as hard and as fast as we can to make sure as many people as possible can be there for what promises to be a truly special moment in Australian music.”

Hailing from Brisbane, the 2032 Olympic City, the ‘Finger, as they’re affectionately known in these parts, was one of the elite bands of their era, one that produced five consecutive ARIA No. 1 albums, 18 ARIA Awards and three APRA Awards, including a brace for song of the year.

Powderfinger called time with that 34-date national trek back in 2010. The music never stopped. When triple j invited Australians to vote for the greatest homegrown songs of all time, for a countdown in July 2025, Powderfinger clocked up more songs in the top 100 (four, including a Fanning solo number) than any other act.
Still elite. And proof, perhaps, that the band’s music had become the soundtrack, too, for younger generations that never saw them in action.

When the classic lineup of Bernard Fanning (vocals), Ian Haug (guitars), Darren Middleton (guitars), John “JC” Collins (bass) and Jon Coghill (drums) hit the road, they’ll do so with an all-Australian lineup, performing in green spaces under a “big tent.”
“We are still gobsmacked by the response to this tour,” comments Fanning on behalf of his bandmates.

“A few weeks ago I was in the ballot for Radiohead tickets. It was BLOODY STRESSFUL and I was eventually lucky enough to be able to buy some. So I understand what a difficult process it can be when you’re trying to juggle work, kids and life in general. So, we are going to put together another string of shows in select destinations that allows as many people as possible to get their hands on tickets.”

Powderfinger’s 2027 tour will partner with Mission Australia, an organization that supports the most vulnerable people in the country. Dew Process Artist Management, Cornershop Agency and Live Nation are partnering on the trek.
“Please keep the faith and be patient,” says Fanning to fans eager to secure a ticket to the show. “We are just as excited to see YOU as you are to see us.”

Oct. 21 (UPI) -- Florida executed a 77-year-old Vietnam veteran for the 1986 fatal shooting of an Indian River County sheriff's deputy, marking the 18th death row inmate to be killed by the state and the 32nd to have their death sentence carried out nationwide this year.

William Reaves was executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison in Raiford, located about 45 miles southwest of Jacksonville, on Tuesday evening. He was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. EDT, the Florida Department of Corrections said in a statement.
"The execution took place without incident," Florida Department of Corrections spokesman Jordan Kirkland told reporters following the execution.
Reaves was executed for killing Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski, 29, early Sept. 23, 1986, outside a Zippy Mart near Vero Beach.

According to court documents, after a reported night of drinking alcohol and smoking and snorting cocaine, Reaves left his girlfriend's house and went to the convenience store, where he called 911 from a payphone to arrange a ride home shortly after 3 a.m. Raczkoski responded to the call and while the two were talking, a .38-caliber pistol fell from the waistband of Reaves' shorts.

The court documents state Raczkoski put his knee on the gun, but Reaves -- a convicted felon who could face additional prison time for having the weapon -- pushed the deputy off the pistol and grabbed it.
Raczkoski managed to turn and run. Reaves fired the entire seven-round clip, hitting Raczkoski four times.
Reaves fled the scene to the home of a friend, telling him that Raczkoski had begged him not to shoot.

"One of us got to go. One of us got to go, me or you," Reaves told Raczkoski, according to the friend, Erman Eugene Hinton, who testified during the trial that Reaves recounted the confrontation to him.
Raczkoski later died on the operating table at the hospital.

Reaves was convicted of premeditated first-degree murder and sentenced to death in 1987. But the Florida Supreme Court reversed his conviction in 1991 as the state prosecutor had represented Reaves as a public defender in an earlier grand larceny case.
He was convicted of murder during a second trial, held in 1992, and again sentenced to death following a 10-2 jury recommendation.
The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeals last week, with the U.S. Supreme Court doing the same shortly before his scheduled 6 p.m. Tuesday execution.

Reaves had acknowledged his responsibility in the shooting, but his lawyers contented that he was suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from his time fighting in the Vietnam War. A defense psychologist testified during the penalty phase of his retrial that Reaves perceived his encounter with Raczkoski as life-threatening.

"Both men swore an oath to protect and defend," Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty said in a statement following the execution, referring to Raczkoski as a sheriff's deputy and Reaves, who volunteered to fight in Vietnam.
"Corporal Raczkoski deserved to go home to his family after his shift ended that night. William Reaves deserved treatment, compassion and understanding for his war wounds. Both things are true."
Reaves' final meal was crackers and juice and he had no final statement.
During a press conference that followed the execution, Raczkoski's brother, Marc Raczkoski, offered one sentence: "I would just like to say that Richard finally has justice and this is put to rest."
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who witnessed the execution, said he thanked Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier "for finally getting this done."
"The last thing this murderer saw was our uniform, was this badge," he said, holding up a sheriff's deputy badge, which he then presented to Marc Raczkoski.
Flowers told the reporters, whom he anticipated would ask his reaction to the execution, that he was "pretty mad."

"He chose not to give a final statement. He chose to have crackers and juice today under the idea that he was was taking communion. Okay. Alright. How about saying something to the family? You admitted to this; how about saying I'm sorry? How about giving us something here? I'll tell you this: Watching that, it was awfully humane for somebody who took somebody's life so recklessly. Pretty disappointed," he said.

"Mark says justice; closure's my word. We have closure because he's gone but I don't think there's any justice in what took place. ... Would we all be so lucky to be 77 years old and die so peacefully. That's not justice in my opinion."
Florida is scheduled to execute Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. 5, for the 2004 murder of Jackie Malone.
If carried out, it will be the state's 19 execution of the year, tying its modern-day record set last year.

Oct. 20 (UPI) -- Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola virus and Kenya its ninth on Tuesday amid a multi-country outbreak that has sickened nearly 10,000 in five countries in less than six months.
The Nigerian Ministry of Health and Social Welfare said in a statement that the patient was a woman who had recently arrived in Nigeria aboard an international flight from Uganda.

It was unclear when she arrived in the country, but Health and Social Welfare Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said she developed symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in the Nigerian capital of Abuja on Oct. 11, Voice of Nigeria reported.
She received care for several days before the diagnosis was confirmed, the ministry statement said, adding that the patient is in isolation and receiving care.

Health workers with the ministry and the Nigerian Center for Disease Control and Prevention have begun contact tracing, with 44 people who may have been exposed to the virus already identified and being monitored, the ministry said. Healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts were among those listed.
"Surveillance has been intensified and the hospital is receiving immediate support to strengthen infection prevention and control measures," the ministry said.

Health officials did not state what virus caused the woman's Ebola infection, but the confirmed case comes amid a multi-country Ebola outbreak caused by the rare and severe Bundibugyo virus, which has infected nearly 10,000 people and killed more than 4,600 in now five countries.

The earliest suspected patient of the outbreak was a healthcare worker in the Democratic Republic of Congo who developed symptoms in late April and subsequently died. the DRC declared an outbreak on May 15.
It has reported more than 9,552 cases, including more than 4,600 deaths, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Kenya's confirmation on Tuesday came two days after it had confirmed its eighth case.

Ministry health officials said in a statement that all nine patients were within a single known cluster. The other eight patients were improving, it said, adding that 134 of 135 contacts have been traced and quarantined.
"There is no evidence of transmission outside the group," the ministry statement said.
Uganda has confirmed 20 cases and two deaths, as well as one probable case and death, but declared itself Ebola free at the end of July. Uganda's last Ebola patient was discharged July 16.

France also confirmed a case, an intensive care doctor who was returning to France from a mission to the DRC in late June. The doctor fully recovered and was discharged. Five low-risk contacts were identified an no further cases were diagnosed.
Nigeria previously experienced an Ebola outbreak in 2014, while this is Kenya's first.

The World Health Organization is urging countries in the region to sustain a high level or readiness, which its director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said was "essential to detect cases early, prevent onward transmission and protect health workers and communities."

Oct. 20 (UPI) -- U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance announced a $25 million whistleblower program Tuesday that they said will pay cash to people who tip off the federal government about those committing fraud.
At the announcement at the Oval Office, Trump said he will be the sole arbitrator of who receives the payouts as part of the Justice Department's Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program.

"I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions," Trump told reporters at the event, The Guardian reported. "In other words, I'll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous,believe me."
The program offers a 1% commission to those who provide a tip that leads to a successful conviction. Anyone can submit a tip to America.gov/fraud, Trump said.
The website said the program could lead to up to $30,000 as an award, but the president said Tuesday that there is "no limit." He also said the payouts only apply "if we recover the money."
"People will make millions of dollars by turning others in," he said, The Hill reported.
The Justice Department website, however, said that department has "sole discretion" in issuing the awards. Trump's actual role was not clear.

The program gave the first award to Nick Shirley, a conservative YouTuber who was also at the event Tuesday. Shirley's videos went viral earlier in 2026 after he accused Somali-run child-care centers in Minnesota of fraud.

Shirley's claims had largely been debunked, although federal agents have continued the investigations and one woman has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the United States. Fox News reported that Shirley received a $10,000 payout Tuesday.
The whistleblower program is to build on the work of Vance's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, which Trump created in March.
"The president has said it must stop," Vance said Tuesday of fraud. "It is stopping, and if you want to help us stop it, you get to share in the rewards now."

On April 15, Ron Wallace tucked a small seed into the soil in his greenhouse in Greene, Rhode Island. Nearly six months later, that seed had grown into a massive pumpkin—one so big it would set a new world record.

On October 10, Wallace’s enormous gourd officially weighed in at 3,156 pounds at the Southern New England Giant Pumpkin Growers Weigh-Off, becoming the first pumpkin to ever top 3,000 pounds. Wallace now holds the Guinness World Record for the heaviest pumpkin, smashing the nearly 2,857-pound record set just a week earlier.

Wallace was introduced to the hobby by his dad, who he says was one of the first New Englanders to grow giant pumpkins, according to a statement. Decades later, he still loves seeing people’s reactions when they encounter one of these gargantuan gourds.

“You ever see anybody say a bad word about a pumpkin?” he tells the New York Times’ Victor Mather. “When you see one of these giants, everybody is just in awe. They want to touch it. They want to sit on it. They want to get photos with it.”
He adds: “A giant pumpkin brings a smile to everybody’s face, and it doesn’t matter where you’re from, what nationality you are. Giant pumpkins don’t care about any of that.”

This isn’t the first time Wallace has grown a record-setting pumpkin. In 2006, he grew a 1,502-pounder, the first to break 1,500 pounds, according to the statement. He reached another milestone in 2012 with a 2,009-pound pumpkin, the first to surpass 2,000 pounds.

Those two previous world records were “historic accomplishments at the time, but this one feels a bit more special,” Wallace says in the statement. “I had a few off growing years as I was taking a more scientific approach. It felt great to see it all come together.”

This year, Wallace’s victory was decisive. While growers typically top the current champion by just 20 to 30 pounds, his pumpkin topped the previous record—set by British grower Ian Paton on October 3—by nearly 300 pounds.

You might think there’d be some bad blood between such fierce competitors. But Wallace and Paton are friends who talk “weekly, sometimes daily” during the growing season, Wallace tells the Providence Journal’s Mark Patinkin. In fact, it was Paton who first suggested that Wallace should try growing his pumpkins in a greenhouse.

Wallace took the advice, and it paid off. Growing his record-setting gourd in a greenhouse this year allowed him to control everything from the amount of water it got to the temperatures it endured. At its peak, his pumpkin was putting on “60 pounds a day, sometimes almost 500 pounds a week,” he tells the Providence Journal.

But it wasn’t just the greenhouse that gave Wallace an edge this season. He also credits “top of the line genetics” and a collaborative, pumpkin-growing community that generously shares tips and tricks to help propel the entire hobby forward, he tells the Times.

When it finally came time to transport his colossal masterpiece to the annual pumpkin weigh-off, Wallace used a harness and a heavy-duty rope to carefully lift the pumpkin off the ground. His team swaddled it in damp sheets, a comforter and shrink wrap, then loaded it onto a custom pallet on the back of a flatbed truck.

Wallace’s pumpkin faced off against roughly 20 other competitors at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island. Upon arrival, his was clearly the largest, and he suspected it might weigh more than 3,000 pounds. But he had no idea how big it really was until it was loaded onto the scale.
“I don’t weigh them,” he tells the Times. “It would be like opening up your gifts before Christmas.”
Once it was weighed, he tells the Associated Press’ Terry Chea and Mikella Schuettler, “the place just exploded.”

What’s next for Wallace’s gigantic gourd? It’s on a victory lap of sorts, with stops at festivals in Pennsylvania and Massachusetts, as well a future as the world’s largest jack-o’-lantern. Once all the pomp has faded away, the pumpkin will meet a fate that befalls most of its smaller fellow gourds and end up in a compost pile.
Wallace will save some of the pumpkin’s seeds, which he plans to donate to pumpkin-growing clubs around the world to auction off for fundraising efforts.
Wallace never imagined a day when pumpkins would top 3,000 pounds—so he has no idea what their upper limit might be.
“Let somebody else chase it for a year, he tells the Providence Journal. “If someone breaks it, I’ll get back at it.”
When humans need to feel rejuvenated, they touch grass. When corals need to recover from bleaching, they should touch a healthy clone, according to new research.

Lab experiments suggest that bleached coral can bounce back within weeks of coming into physical contact with a colorful, genetically identical piece of itself. While the remarkable healing method, published on October 14 in the journal Science Advances, likely can’t restore all the world’s sick corals on its own, the discovery could help inspire new recovery strategies.

“We were blown away [to] actually watch the healthy coral restore the color of the bleached corals essentially right before our eyes,” lead author Danny Collins, a marine biologist at Stanford University, tells KQED’s Danielle Venton. “It was so much faster and more intense than we ever expected.”

Most corals are colonies of small animals called polyps. Polyps in one colony have the same genetics, meaning they are clones of one another. When their watery environment gets too warm too fast, corals lose the colorful, beneficial algae in their tissues that provide energy. Without these vital partners, corals starve, are susceptible to harmful algae, and grow pale—hence the term bleached. Total recovery, if possible, can take months to years.

But in 2025, study co-author and Stanford marine scientist Steve Palumbi stumbled upon a strange possible cure. A healthy hunk of coral had accidentally tipped over and was touching a bleached piece from the same colony in a laboratory tank. At their point of contact, the pale fragment had regained its color, meaning the beneficial algae had returned.

Meanwhile, Collins had been brainstorming about how dangerous bacteria can enter corals when contaminated materials, like plastic debris, touch them. He wondered if researchers could leverage this phenomenon to help corals instead.

“Harmful bacteria enter corals through physical contact,” Collins explains in a statement. “We were curious about what would happen if we used contact to reintroduce something good—the beneficial algae from healthy corals.”

So, the team tested the idea with ten coral fragment pairs—each with one bleached and one colorful piece roughly 1.5 inches long—from the same colony. Half were set up so the sick and healthy fragments were touching, while the others had a millimeters-wide gap between the two branches. All bleached corals touching healthy clones fully healed within seven weeks, but the bleached fragments in non-touching pairs fared poorly, and some died.

“What was most exciting about this was seeing the remarkable potential that bleached corals have to rapidly recover,” Collins tells SFGate’s Anna FitzGerald Guth. “These bleached corals are often treated as a lost cause.”

Taking a closer look under a high-powered microscope revealed that physical contact between two coral clones allowed them to align little channels in their tissues. The healthy coral could then send beneficial algae and nutrients to the stressed one. The team saw transferred material in sick corals after just three days of contact.

What’s more, the fragments didn’t have to touch for the entire duration of the recovery. After roughly one week of contact, bleached corals could disconnect and continue recovering independently. Separated fragments even recovered at the same rate as coral pairs that stayed together. Further experiments revealed that the speedy recovery was largely thanks to algae replicating at record-setting rates inside the sick coral, rather than continuous transfer from the healthy coral.

While the discovery is exciting, it won’t directly translate into a recovery method in the wild, Collins tells Agence France-Presse’s Issam Ahmed. “We likely will not be touching corals to each other on reefs,” he says. It’s impractical to create healthy clones of all corals before bleaching events, per KQED.

Additionally, the solution won’t help dead corals, Terry Hughes, a marine biologist at James Cook University in Australia who wasn’t involved in the study, tells the New York Times’ Raymond Zhong. He adds that the best way to aid corals is to reduce emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases.

The findings are still “super interesting,” says Andrea Grottoli, a coral researcher at Ohio State University who also wasn’t involved in the study, to the outlet. She says that the work could pave the way to “more organic” ways to help corals. Reefs are invaluable marine habitats. Even though they make up merely 0.01 percent of the ocean floor, they support about a quarter of all sea life.

The British Empire was undoubtedly global. Beginning in the 16th century, its economic dominance was made possible, in large part, by maritime merchants and business-minded seafarers. By force, deals and persuasion, it built a vast network of overseas colonies, connecting the isle to distant shores and its people with coveted commodities, including tea from India, sugarcane from Jamaica and tobacco from Virginia.

But new research suggests that a reliable web of shorter routes within Britain and with other European countries accounted for a significant majority of the nation’s trade—more than its colonies across the globe—as its empire grew between the late-16th and mid-18th centuries. Between 1696 and 1697, for example, a whopping 80 percent of the value of Britain’s global trade was generated by European markets.

“It’s interesting to note that even centuries ago, Europe was Britain’s principal overseas trading region, and although Britain had important global connections, most of its core trade was still being done closer to its own shores,” John McAleer, a historian at the University of Southampton and the project’s co-lead, says in a statement.

The project’s findings—published in a first-of-its-kind searchable online database—chart the empire’s growth and trade according to the data stored in hundreds of thousands of pages of port books, handwritten customs records of British ships, routes, destinations and cargo from 1565 onwards.

Researchers used artificial intelligence (AI) to help comb through the vast contents of the delicate parchment pages stored in the British National Archives. They trained software to decipher port officials’ unique handwriting styles, identify idiosyncratic notations and adapt to how the spelling of certain words changed over time.

“Without AI extracting and organizing the data, this would have taken years,” Craig Lambert, a historian at the University of Southampton and the project’s lead researcher, says in the statement. “It still needed manual checking, but it sped up the process enormously.”

In the maritime database, users can search for specific routes by ship name, commodity, port of origin, destination or year, and then trace the visual outline of the exact routes that vessels once followed on a digital map produced by the university’s GeoData Institute.

Analysis of these records revealed a bustling network of more than 3,000 ports across the world, including more than 1,000 domestic ports in Britain. A plurality (426) were located in southwest Britain and another 306 were found on the southeastern coast. But every maritime location played an important role. Those in Hull and Whitby, for example, on England’s eastern shores, were critical trading posts for exchanges with the Netherlands and Scandinavia.

“The Baltic is rich in grain, but it’s also rich in timber,” Lambert says in a video. “And that’s what the British need in vast quantities for the shipbuilding programs that they’re undertaking in this period.”

Ports located further north, including Newcastle and Sunderland, were key nodes in the coal trade, which powered the Industrial Revolution. Coal was the most commonly traded commodity that the researchers analyzed, appearing in more than 101,000 cargo entries. Malt, wheat, iron, wool and wine were the next-most popular goods.

“Much of England’s shipping was not engaged in glamorous long-distance voyages to the Americas or Asia,” Lambert tells the London Times’ Rhys Blakely. “Coastal shipping was fundamental to the economy, carrying coal, grain and other essential commodities between English ports.”

Over the roughly 200-year timeframe the researchers analyzed, British ships connected with 157 maritime sites in France, 68 in the Netherlands and 59 in India. Overall, of Britain’s top 15 trading partners by number of recorded maritime locations, 10 were on the continent.

Still, the more unique imports that appear in the ledgers—children’s toys from China, exotic animal skins and Venice treacle, an ancient medicine believed to cure nearly any ailment—hint at the empire’s globalizing reach.

In the late 1800s, Westminster Abbey clergy stumbled upon a mysterious sarcophagus. The lid was decorated with an 11th-century Anglo-Saxon cross, but the base had a fourth-century Roman funeral inscription. For nearly 150 years, the tomb has baffled experts, but the abbey's consulting archaeologist may have finally figured out who was buried there, according to a new study.

Westminster's chief mason unearthed the stone sarcophagus in 1869, but when experts investigated it, they discovered that the burial had been looted earlier that century. Experts also noticed that the carved decoration on the side of the sarcophagus was stylistically Roman, with a Latin inscription that can be translated as "To the memory of Valerius Amandinus. Valerius Superventor and Marcellus made this for their father." But an enormous medieval cross had been carved into the lid of the sarcophagus, suggesting that the tomb had been reused to bury an important religious figure hundreds of years later.

The mystery of the medieval individual buried in a Roman sarcophagus remained unsolved for 150 years, as no one thought that any bones were left inside. But when the stone coffin was opened for conservation in 2016 and a full skeleton was discovered, clues to the identity of the deceased finally came to light, Warwick Rodwell, the consultant archaeologist for Westminster Abbey, wrote in a study published Wednesday (Oct. 21) in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association.

Although the skeleton had been disturbed over the years, with a hole accidentally made in the skull and arm and leg bones mixed up, it was clear that the person was male, middle-aged, and of average height, bioarchaeologist James Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology wrote in a 2016 report. The man also had some evidence of osteoarthritis, two healed rib injuries and gout. The bones were carbon-dated to between 987 and 1052, confirming that the Roman-era sarcophagus was reused in the Middle Ages.
The Roman-era sarcophagus was reworked in the Middle Ages to include a cross on the top. It is on display in Westminster Abbey.
There is a Latin inscription on the side of the Roman-era sarcophagus in Westminster Abbey.
Archaeologists think that the sarcophagus was originally discovered in the burial pit near the sacristy.
An overview of the interior of the sarcophagus, with the disordered skeleton of a medieval abbot.
The abbot's skull was damaged in the past and then reconstructed using wire and glue before being put back in the sarcophagus.

"This brings us to the final question of importance: who was he?" Rodwell wrote in the study. Despite the lack of grave goods, which may have been stolen in the early 19th century, "he was almost certainly an abbot" who was given a dignified burial in a stone sarcophagus with a large cross, Rodwell wrote.

Based on the birth and death dates of the abbots of Westminster and their tenure as clergy, Rodwell narrowed the candidates down to Wulfsige (abbot from 988 to 993), Ælfwig (abbot from 993 to 1020) and Wulfnoth (abbot from 1020 to 1049). Given that Wulfsige left Westminster to become a bishop elsewhere, he was likely not buried in the abbey.
"Consequently, we have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus," Rodwell wrote. "The fact that Ælfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favour him."

Although the final resting place of Ælfwig may have been found after a millennium, some questions remain unanswered.

For example, it is unclear why an 11th-century abbot was buried in a recycled fourth-century Roman sarcophagus. The reuse of Roman coffins is extremely unusual, Rodwell noted in the study, and nothing comparable to this sarcophagus has ever been found. One explanation for the reuse may rest with the Latin inscription, whose first word — "memoriae" (to the memory) — suggests that Valerius Amandinus was an early Christian himself. This Roman may have been a significant figure in Roman London, Rodwell wrote, but "unfortunately, nothing is known about his career."

Experts are also unsure where the Roman sarcophagus came from. It was made from limestone sourced from Oxfordshire, a county in the South of England. But perhaps the coffin was originally buried in a Roman mausoleum and they were unearthed and moved at some point, Rodwell noted. But as Rodwell pointed out in the study, "there could be a villa and its cemetery somewhere in the vicinity of Westminster Abbey, awaiting discovery."
The sarcophagus is currently on display in the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.

Some people with depression sleep far more than average, wake up exhausted, habitually stay up late, and experience mood shifts with the seasons. A new study suggests that these symptoms may cluster in a distinct subtype of depression that's tied to the body's internal clock.

While research has long linked a scrambled circadian rhythm to a risk of mood disorders, neuroscientists are now proposing that these disruptions define a specific form of depression that they call "circadian depression." First conceptualized in 2021, the body-clock subtype may affect about 1 in 4 people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, the researchers estimate.
In their new study, published Wednesday (Oct. 21) in The British Journal of Psychiatry, the team identified the subtype in about 2,600 people out of over 11,000 evaluated.

"Circadian depression is a biologically informed subtype," said study co-author Emiliana Tonini, a neuroscientist at the University of Sydney. "Unlike subtypes defined mainly by symptoms, the core feature here is a disturbed circadian system, which common antidepressants may not fully address," Tonini told Live Science in an email.

The researchers think treatments that target the sleep-wake system, such as the sleep hormone melatonin or bright light therapy, might be beneficial for people with this subtype. However, because the subtype is still a proposal and not formally established yet, other experts say that further research is needed before the findings can inform clinical practice.

Tonini and her team analyzed data from 11,380 adults ages 18 to 90 who took part in the Australian Genetics of Depression Study (AGDS), a nationwide study exploring how genes and life experiences influence depression and responses to treatment. They classified participants under the "circadian" umbrella if they had at least three of six features: seasonal mood swings, late sleep schedules, social jet lag (a mismatch between sleep routine during workdays and free days), night-owl habits, excessive sleep (hypersomnia), and fatigue upon waking.

A total of 2,604 people fit the proposed subtype. Compared with others in the AGDS cohort, this group was younger and developed depression earlier in life — around 19, compared with about 23 for the rest of the cohort.

The group also skewed female, and individuals reported greater psychological distress, frequent suicidal thoughts and more physical complaints than people who didn't fit the proposed subtype. Some experienced weight gain during depressive episodes and symptoms resembling hypomania, a revved-up state of elevated mood and energy that's milder than full-blown mania.

However, having this constellation of symptoms doesn't mean someone's biological clock is disrupted, said Brant Hasler, a psychologist and sleep researcher at the University of Pittsburgh who was not involved in the study. The researchers relied on the participants' self-reports of their sleep patterns; that data correlates only modestly with direct measures of circadian timing, such as measurements of melatonin in saliva, he said in an email.
"One can identify as an evening-type, and report later sleep timing, and still have physiological circadian timing that is not particularly delayed," he said.

So, in addition to checking symptoms, the team hunted for genetic clues underlying the proposed subtype. They analyzed DNA from participants' saliva samples and calculated "polygenic risk scores," which add up the influence of thousands of different genetic variants to estimate how likely someone is to develop a given condition.
"Mental health conditions are shaped by hundreds or thousands of variants that each add a small amount of risk, so everyone carries a unique 'portfolio' of risk," Tonini explained.

People in the circadian group had a higher genetic risk for depression, anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and bipolar disorder, the analysis suggested. They also had a greater genetic risk of higher body weight, insulin resistance, inflammation, insomnia and late-night sleep habits, compared with the other study participants.
This suggests "circadian depression is more than just 'depression with bad sleep,'" Tonini said. "It involves a mix of metabolic, inflammatory, circadian, and mood-related processes."

The researchers looked at the participants' past experiences with antidepressants, finding that the circadian group reported less benefit from common medications, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). Common examples include the SSRI Lexapro and the SNRI Cymbalta.
The circadian group also experienced more side effects from these treatments, such as drowsiness, nausea, anxiety and weight gain.

"If circadian disruption is a core biological mechanism in these individuals, treatments that fail to address those abnormalities may naturally be less effective," said Dr. Ruth Benca, a psychiatrist and sleep researcher at Wake Forest University School of Medicine who was not involved in the study. However, Benca cautioned that body-clock disruption may not be the only reason standard drugs fall short for these patients.

"People with more pronounced circadian disturbances often have more severe illness and other psychiatric conditions, which can contribute to treatment resistance," Benca told Live Science in an email.

Even so, tracking sleep, measurements of circadian rhythm, and seasonal shifts in mood could help clinicians identify at-risk patients earlier and select more effective treatments sooner in the course of illness, Benca suggested. "Potential approaches include behavioral routines, structured sleep schedules, or chronotherapy," in which the timing of medication or light exposure is strategically coordinated with internal body rhythms, she added.

Clinical trials are still needed to draw firm conclusions about potential treatments, Tonini noted. The findings also must be validated in broader populations, since the study drew on a single Australian cohort and its genetic analysis included only people of European ancestry.
For now, "the study is an important step toward a more personalized treatment approach," she said.

Flying cars once seemed like the stuff of science fiction. But Tesla's recent demonstration, which showed the company's Rocket Roadster model briefly flying, has reignited the conversation about whether flying cars could soon become a reality.

The technology behind flying cars is continuing to advance, with companies developing vehicles that combine elements of traditional cars, helicopters, electric aircraft, and — in Tesla's case — rockets. Many of these designs use electric vertical-takeoff-and-landing technology, which allows them to lift off and land without a runway by using multiple rotors or propellers to generate lift. Advances in battery technology, autonomous flight systems and computer-assisted navigation are helping to make these vehicles seem more feasible. But challenges remain, including questions surrounding passenger safety, affordability, and the need for regulations and laws and infrastructure for the widespread use of these vehicles.

Tesla says production of its new "flying car" is scheduled for 2028, but the company is notorious for not meeting its proposed deadlines. The automotive suspension market will grow from $39.6 billion in 2026 to $43.2 billion by 2033, according to MarketsandMarkets. The report projects a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 1.2%. The automotive suspension market continues to expand as manufacturers transition from passive mechanical components to electronically controlled, software-coordinated systems.

Increasing adoption of adaptive and semi-active dampers and air suspension allows automakers to optimize ride comfort, handling and body control independently. These technologies reduce reliance on fixed spring-damper characteristics.

Software-defined vehicles and automated driving also increase the need to coordinate suspension with steering, braking and vehicle-motion-control systems. Suppliers such as ZF already integrate active and semi-active damping with centralized chassis software.

Larger battery packs increase vehicle mass and alter weight distribution. Growing SUV and large-vehicle adoption also increases requirements for load management, ride-height control and roll and pitch suppression. These factors support higher-value suspension architectures.

Sensor- and camera-informed predictive suspension offers another growth opportunity. These systems use road-surface information to adjust damping before vehicles encounter disturbances. For example, ZF’s AI Road Sense feeds road-condition data into chassis software to control damping in real time.

However, active and semi-active suspension systems increase complexity, sensor and actuator requirements, functional safety demands and calibration efforts. Automakers must justify higher costs through measurable improvements in ride quality, handling and safety. Scalable architectures and software reuse remain critical for mass-market adoption.
MacPherson Suspensions Expected to Maintain Largest Market Share

MacPherson struts remain the most widely adopted front-suspension architecture globally. Asia-Pacific represents the largest market by volume because of high production of compact and midsize passenger cars and light commercial vehicles (LCVs).

Low costs, compact packaging, simplified components and reduced weight make MacPherson struts suitable for high-volume vehicle platforms. Eliminating a separate upper control arm also reduces weight while maintaining adequate ride and handling performance.
Estimates indicate MacPherson struts accounted for more than 70% of compact and midsize vehicle front-suspension applications in 2025. This estimate covers China, India and Southeast Asia.

Compatibility with modular vehicle platforms allows automakers to standardize suspension layouts across multiple models. This reduces engineering, tooling and assembly complexity while supporting internal combustion engine (ICE) and electric vehicle (EV) packaging requirements.

MacPherson suspensions dominate mainstream vehicles across Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America. However, premium SUVs, performance vehicles and higher-end EVs increasingly use double-wishbone or multilink front suspensions. These advanced architectures provide greater wheel control, handling precision and ride refinement.

MacPherson suspensions retain volume leadership in cost-sensitive applications, while advanced architectures serve higher-value vehicles. Suppliers increasingly focus on higher-content MacPherson systems rather than replacing the architecture. These systems incorporate lightweight struts, integrated knuckles, advanced dampers and electronically controlled modules.
Active Suspension Projected to Experience Fastest Growth

Active suspension represents the fastest-growing suspension segment during the forecast period. Growing demand for ride comfort, handling precision, safety and real-time vehicle dynamics drives adoption, particularly among premium passenger vehicles and SUVs.

In 2025, Asia-Pacific accounted for more than 60% of new-vehicle SUV sales. Higher curb weights and elevated ride heights increase demand for adaptive and active suspension systems. High-end EVs and luxury SUVs increasingly incorporate electronically controlled suspension technologies. Examples include the Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV, Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo and BMW iX.

These systems manage battery-related mass, variable loading, pitch, roll and ride comfort. Active suspensions continuously generate counterforces at each wheel, providing greater body-motion control than passive or semi-active systems.

Integrated chassis control also supports adoption. Active suspension coordinates with steering, braking and torque-vectoring systems to manage pitch, roll, heave and wheel loads independently. These capabilities improve vehicle control during acceleration, braking and cornering.

High-performance EVs and premium SUVs require systems that compensate for greater vehicle mass and rapidly changing axle loads. Manufacturers must maintain ride comfort and handling despite these demands.
Predictive Suspension Technologies Gain Importance

Camera-based advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and road-preview technologies support predictive suspension development. These technologies detect road disturbances before wheels encounter them and proactively adjust actuator force. This shifts suspension technology from reactive damping toward software-controlled vehicle-motion management.

Integrating sensors, ADAS and software-defined vehicle platforms also enables predictive damping and load-sensitive suspension control. These developments increase the importance of software and electronic components within suspension systems.

Suppliers can differentiate their products through adaptive control, software calibration and integrated vehicle-dynamics functions. These capabilities also help premium automakers distinguish their EV and SUV driving experiences.

Hunter Engineering announced four new enhancements to its HawkEye XL Commercial Alignment System.
The new enhancements include (with descriptions by the company):

1) Magnetic wheel adapters – These adapters provide increased wheel protection, with no metal spades to get between the rim and tire, the company says. The adapters are available as an option for new and existing HawkEyeXL aligners.

2) Drive-through sensor configuration – The new configuration will allow drive-through shops and OEM production to skip repositioning their equipment for each alignment. The sensors offer the same long-range vision and field of view, with up to 16-foot-wide tower spacing to accommodate commercial vehicles.

3) New WinAlign software – Hunter’s latest WinAlign 18.3 software offers new target placement guidance to help the technician, aligner placement guidance so the cameras can easily see all the wheel targets, and the flexibility to perform thrustline and frame-reference alignments as desired.

4) Latest-generation alignment cart – Technicians can store adapters and control the alignment system from the rear of the vehicles. The cart is completely untethered with a battery backup, allowing a full day’s work without carrying a cable around the shop, the company says.
The XL handles heavy-duty, medium-duty, light-duty and passenger vehicles.
